The unanimous consent given, as I understood it, was a consent that my hon. friend should get his interim supply, -but that he should confine it to interim supply, and not ask the House to go through the form of taking all the different estimates that have already been passed and of asking for concurrences.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: The usual course is that we take all the estimates that have been dealt with and add one-sixth of the remainder. I think that is the invariable practice. If that is not so, I shall have to let the matter stand over until to-morrow and re-cast the resolution.

What we used to do, and what my hon. friend always took objection to, was to vote one-sixth, full right being reserved to object, later on, to any estimates that had not already been passed. We have to-day some important matters that, I think, should not lose their right of way for the purpose of concurring in everything that has been voted. I am perfectly willing to consent to all that we thought would be done, namely, that the government should have the necessary interim supply, and we consent to a resolution now going through for one-sixth, the usual supply, as interim supply, without prejudice to the opposition or anybody else who may wish to object to any individual item.

Mr. PIERRE F. CASGRAIN (Charlevoix-Montmorency) moved:
That, in the opinion of this House, in view of the fact that the Bankruptcy Act, 1919, and amendments thereto, does not obtain the results expected, and is the source of complaints from various industries and trades, it is desirable that the said law should be amended or abrogated.
He said: Mr. Speaker, last year I had on the order paper a resolution similar to this but I did not press it because I was given to understand that substantial amendments would be introduced to the Bankruptcy Act. The amendments, however, which were bought down in the last lap of the session, were of not much importance; they did net cover many of the points discussed and did not appear at any rate to be such as to afford relief.
All over the country to-day, especially in the province of Quebec, the present law and its application is criticized. Its enforcement during the last three years has been sufficient to prove to the general public that the law is not as good as it was thought it would be, not even as good as the old system which formerly prevailed under the abandonment of property provisions in our province and the Winding-up Act. Everybody will understand that the bankruptcy law is of the highest importance; it has a great influence on the economic and commercial life of the country, and even, I would add, on its morality. When our present law was passed one of its objects was to provide that when a person became insolvent his wealth and property should belong to his creditors and be distributed among them equitably; that a debtor was to be liberated if he were not proved guilty of any fraud, and that the costs were to be reduced to a minimum. That is what we were told when the provisions of the present law were introduced in the House in 1919 and that had been the object of previous laws respecting bankruptcy in this country. Since its enforcement, however, the present law seems to have

Bankruptcy
opened the door to fraud and speculation. It has been injurious to the credit of individuals and commercial firms and in large measure has contributed to the financial depression that at present exists in this country. There is a good deal of feeling against the law, not only in the province of Quebec but also in other parts of the Dominion. And just here I cannot do better, Mr. Speaker, than to cite to the House some remarks made by Mr. Colby, then member for Stanstead, when the law of 18S0 was repealed. He said:
The idea of protecting the honest and unfortunate debtor was a humane and proper idea, but in England, in the United States and in Canada, where endeavours have been made to protect the honest and unfortunate trader, the door had been unfortunately opened to fraud, demoralization, recklessness, and evils so numerous that it became necessary in the public interest, that these facilities should be done away with.
This seems to have been the case in connection with the present law. I believe also that the promoters of the law, who were desirous of having uniform legislation on the subject- and I am told that the idea originated in the western provinces, the Canadian Credit Men's Association being its chief promoter-have had fault to find with it since it went into force. Mr. Detchon, the general manager of that association, is reported as having said recently that the law is favourable to the dishonest trader who makes use of the same to get rid of his indebtedness and in a certain way to keep the greatest part of his money to the detriment of his creditors. In the province of Quebec numerous trustees have been appointed under this law, and their aim and object has been to show people financially embarrassed the way to get out of their difficulties. We have seen circulars issued to people of the trades and industries and to others, asking them to call meetings of their officers or trustees for the purpose of discussing methods of overcoming their financial difficulties of the moment and of trying to get rid of their debt and turning over a new leaf. These people have sent notices out and have employed canvassers not only in the cities but in the country districts as well. We have seen many of them in the province of Quebec going to honest farmers in certain communities who are in some little financial difficulty and offering to fix things up for them. They tell these farmers that if they will let them look after their affairs they will put them under the provisions of the Bankruptcy Act so that they may have freedom from all their creditors. I am told that a great many people in the rural districts have been lured by these canvassers who told them that their financial difficulties would be relieved, and
the result has been that they have run into further difficulties. Sometimes they have succeeded in paying only 10, 15 or 20 per cent and have not been any better off after they failed; in fact, their position has been worse.
The present law provides facilities to enable the debtor to go to a trustee, open all his affairs to him, and ask him to make a settlement. In my opinion too much freedom is thus allowed to the debtor who is not so scrupulous, because he can go to a trustee and by preparing a -statement of his affairs from two to six months ahead he can make a showing which, while substantially according to the facts, is not fully accurate and may thus make an attempt to get away with something.
I may be told that there is a provision in the law under which such a trustee may be removed. It is true that a trustee may be removed for cause after a meeting of creditors called for the purpose. But it is usually the case that when a man goes to the trouble of getting a trustee to look after his affairs for him he has beforehand sought the opinion of some of the largest creditors and obtained their consent to the arrangement on the understanding that those creditors will get off not too badly and that they will be paid a certain amount of their claim. 'Then when an attempt is made to put out the trustees who have been so chosen, the creditors who have not been consulted find themselves in the dark; they are without support, and thus there cannot be secured the number of creditors necessary to bring about the removal of the trustees. This is one of the bad features of the law. In Montreal and in the rural districts as well people have failed who would have been able to meet their indebtedness with a little effort ; they could have found a remedy for their financial difficulties without taking a course that would leave their creditors with nothing.
The cost of operations under the present law is too great. One of the objects of the [DOT] law, as was stated on its introduction, was to reduce the costs of legal services and of trustees. I had a case in court where the creditors had taken proceedings against a debtor, obtained judgment and the property was in the hands of the sheriff to be sold. The cost amounted to about $300. Just a day or so before the date fixed for the sale, the trustee went to the debtor and explained the situation to him. The debtor immediately made an assignment, took the benefit of the law, and the costs were useless. Now the assets of the estate have been wound up, and the costs will have to be paid by the creditors for proceedings against the debtor, although the proceedings were of no avail. The creditors will lose the costs they have paid.
Bankruptcy

We had another case in which the assets of an insolvent debtor realized the sum of $680, and the fees for the proceedings and for the legal advice of the trustees amounted to $527; the balance went to the privileged creditors and the ordinary creditors went away with nothing. Another case was that of Le Union Co-operation des Fcrmiers de St. Leon-le-Grand. The proceeds in that case amounted to $3,943.40, and the cost and disbursements amounted to $2,056.44, leaving a dividend of 8J per cent to the creditors. Today in most of the small cases the costs absorb nearly the whole amount realized, and the ordinary creditors receive hardly anything. So that we are not much more advanced than we were under the old law. Then we have the bill of costs also of the lawyers, and in this case I am not speaking for myself, and I am not trying to unduly protect the lawyer, because some comments were made in this House a few weeks ago that lawyers were crowding the people hard. This law was made to try to prevent abuses. I had occasion to examine bills of cost myself and I find that the bills of cost are just as heavy as before.
Under the old law, in the superior court of the province of Quebec, it would cost us for a petition from $16 to $20-not more than $20-and now the costs under an order amount to $60, $85 or $90. Last year I had occasion to present a petition to a trustee to declare a dividend, and the costs amounted to $85. It is the same case everywhere, and the trustees themselves and the registrar are authorized by this law to charge for each and every single thing they do, and if any hon. member who has a moment to spare would kindly look at the tariff, which is to be found at the end of the sections, he would find that the bailiff, the trustees, the employees and all the assistants of the trustees, are well and favourably protected, much more than they were under the old law, The Winding-up Act and the Judicial Abandonment of Property Act as administered in Quebec before this law was in force.
There is another objection to this law. The law allowed the trader to fail, and by allowing the trader to fail, it has ruined in my opinion the credit of a great many other persons. We saw last year a great many people who would have been able, under other circumstances, to withstand the commercial and industrial depression and meet their liabilities and claims of their creditors, if it had not been for the bankruptcy law which is in force. We have seen many cases where the merchant would have been able to borrow from the 
bank or from individuals to carry on and obtain the necessary amount of money to settle his affairs, but he could not borrow this money on account of the bankruptcy law, because the people would say to him, "We have no guarantee, if we advance you a certain amount of money, that in a few days from now, with the help of some trustees or other creditors, you will not assign, and we will be left in the cold and will have no recourse under the law." Many of these merchants have gone to the banks and tried to borrow money and the banks have refused to lend them money because they were afraid they might assign and the bank would not be protected. Another objection is that a hypothec or mortgage created within three months preceding the insolvency is declared void, and that the creditor under the mortgage or hypothec has not the right to recover, according to the rank of the hypothec. The result is that in our province of Quebec, in farming districts, farmers who have become embarrassed under the old law would have been able to obtain money on their farming property, have found the door closed to them on account of this very same law, because the people did not trust them and they were afraid that the hypothec they would obtain on their property would be declared null and void. Since the law has been in force we have seen many merchants and others refusing to give credit to traders' or other persons on account of this law. The industrial people, trades people, the business men and the manufacturers are all opposed to the law, and it is a strange thing that those who were pressing for this law in 1919 are all now in favour of the proposition that it should be either abrogated or amended in a way to protect the interest of the merchant, the manufacturer and the industrial people.
At a certain meeting of La Chambre de Commerce in Montreal, which is a French institution similar to the Board of- Trade in Ontario, a resolution was passed declaring that La Chambre de Commerce was opposed to the law, and stating that even with the amendments passed at the last session of parliament the law was too wide and more advantageous to the bankrupt.

speechtext: Will the hon. member allow me a question?

speechtext: Yes.

speechtext:
Do I understand the hon. member to say that a mortgage registered within three months prior to an assignment act is invalid, even if it were a bona fide mortgage, and no mala tides?

Bankruptcy

subsubtopic: PROPOSED ABROGATION OR AMENDMENT OF BANKRUPTCY ACT, 1919
speechtext:
I will come to that point. We have in our civil code article 2023 which says that a mortgage registered within thirty days of the insolvency of the debtor, if it is notoriously known that the man is insolvent, is no good. We have also article 2090 which prevents the registration of any mortgage or privilege on the movable property of the debtor within 30 days immediately preceding the insolvency.
Then I say if we have these provisions in our law to protect us and protect the creditors against the insolvent debtors, or the traders who might be in bad circumstances, I do not see why we should have gone to the trouble of enacting in this new law other articles which have made it worse for us, which are cumbersome, and are in a certain way overlapping the law of the province of Quebec.

subsubtopic: PROPOSED ABROGATION OR AMENDMENT OF BANKRUPTCY ACT, 1919
speechtext: Does the bankruptcy law not distinguish between actual money advanced in exchange for a mortgage and the other class where the mortgage is given for a past due debt?

subsubtopic: PROPOSED ABROGATION OR AMENDMENT OF BANKRUPTCY ACT, 1919
speechtext: Well, Mr. Speaker, I am not in a position to answer that question now. I do not think the law makes any distinction as to that, at any rate not that I can remember. I know the law, and it is very complicated and pretty hard to understand. There are lawyers, and many trustees of long standing, in the province of Quebec who are not able to understand it. They find, too, that in many cases, there are contradictions in the law.

subsubtopic: PROPOSED ABROGATION OR AMENDMENT OF BANKRUPTCY ACT, 1919
speechtext: The hon. gentleman will admit there are some lawyers who understand it.

subsubtopic: PROPOSED ABROGATION OR AMENDMENT OF BANKRUPTCY ACT, 1919
speechtext:
My hon. friend no doubt understands the law as he has made a special study of it, just as he has in the case of the Immigration Act. I say that the law, as it is at present framed is not in the interest of the business community and should either be amended or repealed. I am not alone in that belief. I have cited the opinions of the Chambre de Commerce of Montreal and I hope I may be permitted to read a few extracts of what we see every day in the newspapers of our province. When I opened my newspaper some time ago I saw the heading "Bankruptcy Law Operation Flayed." That was the heading over the report of a certain organization, the Old Colony Club, which was meeting at the Windsor hotel in Montreal and trying to find some way out of the existing difficulties either by the improvement of the present law or by its abrogation. A head-'
line in another newspaper was worded "Bankruptcy Act Not Understood." It may be that that is what my hon. friend was drawing my attention to a moment ago. This had reference to a meeting of the local Rotary Club of Montreal at which efforts were made to discover some amendments to the law which it was thought would remedy the existing conditions in the country. The heading over another newspaper article reads "Bankruptcy Law Needs Amendment." So you see that people, not only in the city of Montreal but in other districts of the province, are getting busy and endeavouring to devise some means of amending this law.
I have here also an article which was published in the Montreal Gazette about the time of the opening of the present session, and I quote from that article the folllowing:
The results have been, apparently, advantageous, but not to the creditors. The present law does not differ in principle from its short-lived predecessor of 1875-80; The fault with the old law was attributed to administrative weaknesses, and the new statute was professedly designed to remedy these defects.
And then further on:
The principal objection to the existing law in Canada, as expressed from time to time, is that it does not adequately safeguard the interests of the creditors and of legitimate business, in short, that it makes insolvency profitable to the debtor. It has been criticized further upon the score of expense and upon the ground that it is cumbersome, and the amendments made last year were intended to improve it in these respects.
These amendments did not affect the principle of the law, and do not, apparently, meet the main objection, namely, that the statute encourages bankruptcy. Such an objection, if substantiated, is sufficient to condemn the act, as, obviously, the purpose of the law is frustrated in the result alleged. The case may not be as bad as it is represented to be, but the volume and character of the criticisms denote a fundamental flaw somewhere in the system, and the matter is of sufficient importance to engage the attention of the government and of parliament.
It is for this reason that I am now moving this resolution, in the hope that hon. members will co-operate with me and impress upon the Minister of Justice the importance of making certain desired amendments to the law.
Another effect which this law has had is that it has practically abolished articles 853 and 892 of our code of civil procedure, regarding the abandonment of property, which were in force for fifteen years before they were thus practically superseded and which gave entire satisfaction. Article 891 declares that a debtor is liberated from 4 p.m. debt only up to the extent of the amount that his creditors receive from the proceeds of the sale of his assets. On the other hand section 58 of the new Bankruptcy law states that a bankrupt
Bankruptcy

person may ask and obtain his release if he had not been proven guilty of any fraud, there being however, certain conditions which must be complied with. It is easy to imagine all the abuses that might possibly flow from such a law. Instead of forcing the bankrupt trader to fulfil his obligations and respect his dealings with his creditors, to my mind, this provision encourages the trader to incur further liabilities. There is also the opportunity of indulging in speculation by giving to the unscrupulous trader a chance, after having made some bad bargain, or of indulging in some imprudent dealings, to get free by making a settlement of some kind on easy terms with his creditors. Sometimes creditors, even though they may have sufficient time, are not interested enough in the settlement of their claims. Very often they do not look with sufficient care into these cases when they are brought to their attention, or when they receive a notice to approve or disapprove of an agreement or a settlement. It is too much the custom of such people to say, "I have made a certain amount of money out of this man, I have had certain transactions with him and in most cases he has paid me well; I shall lose a certain amount in the present case but I will let it go at that." In other cases the creditors are discouraged and do not want to spend more time and money in what they look upon as an uncertainty. The consequence is the bankrupt is liberated when he should not be freed at all. Under the old law in our province, which law is still in force, respecting the judicial abandonment of property, only a man who was in danger of arrest on a capias or a trader in a bad financial condition could assign. To-day, under this Dominion law, any person, whether he is a trader or not, can assign. Under article 853 of the provincial law only a debtor who was liable to be arrested, or a trader who had ceased his payments, could make an assignment. To-day, under this Dominion law, any man can do so whether he is a trader, a real estate operator, an engineer, or even a trustee; and I am told that in certain cities there are men acting as trustees who have made compromises with their creditors and who are operating under an extension of time. I am told that such men as these have, unfortunately, been given the administration of certain estates in the district in which they reside. The position of these men might have escaped the notice of the department because of their being highly rcommended. I am, however, informed on good authority that there are such cases and it is hardly necessary to say that such IMr. Casgrain.]
men should not be occupying the position of trustees.
Another objection that I see to the present law is,this: articles 1,999 and 2,005 of our civil code which were made for the protection of the landlord have been, to a certain extent, abrogated and the landlord has not the privilege which he enjoyed under the old law. Under section 52 of the present law the landlord is only granted three months' rental previous to the insolvency. A trustee can occupy the premises from month to month at the same rental, or at a certain rental fixed by the court. The trustee also has the privilege to cancel the lease at any time during the year, and the result is that in many cases the landlord suffers great loss and great inconvenience.
Sections 29 and 48 of the present law also seem to me to be objectionable because they do away with certain features of the clauses of the marriage contract which have been the basis and the mainstay of the family life and of the marital rights as between husband and wife.
Another objection to the law I find in article 85, which deals with the permission given to a company to assign. According to article 85, a company may assign if it is duly represented, and this other paragraph of the law states that a firm has a right to assign by one of its members. I am informed that in Montreal, in the case of Byers and Craig, one of the partners of the firm put the firm into liquidation and judgment was rendered on that point that, according to the article, as it was drafted, there was no other course than to maintain the action of the partner which was supposed to be binding on behalf of the firm. This article should be amended in such a way as to protect a member of a firm who might be put into trouble and lose a good deal of the money he had invested in the firm, if any other member could put the firm into insolvency. The trouble was that when this law was made, it was made to cover and protect creditors in other parts of the country than Quebec which do not seem to have the same provisions that we have in our civil code and code of procedure, and it is for this reason that we see many articles in the law and many things in the rules and regulations which seem to be overlapping and which cause so m,uch trouble, as has been the experience since the law has been in force.
Many insolvencies have occurred recently in Quebec. If you open a newspaper or pass through any of the streets of our cities, what do you see? "Bankruptcy" or "sale judicially authorized." We see this in Montreal, especi-

Bankruptcy
ally. This is due, I believe to the fact that the law renders it too easy to the debtor to avail himself of its provisions. If we consider the many insolvencies that have taken place, we find that most of the insolvencies- at any rate I am so informed as regards the district of Montreal-have been voluntary and that the- debtors themselves have gone to the trustees and arranged their affairs with them and a few of their creditors to try to get away with the matter. We are presented sometimes with a compromise or a certain agreement reached with a number of creditors who have the largest claims, and as I said at the beginning of my remarks, it is pretty hard to upset them. Formerly, it was only the trader who could assign, because he needed credit and he was in business; but to-day any person who is a debtor can make - an assignment. We have also in the law a provision that a debtor can assign, not only in his district, but in other places, and I have seen many cases where debtors of rural districts have assigned in the district of Montreal. One of my hon. friends was pointing out to me that one debtor in the district of Joliette had assigned in another district entirely different from his own. This complicates matters and compels creditors to follow up their debtors to other districts than those in which they ought to assign, as was the case under the old law thereby increasing expenses.

speechtext: No. But before we had that law, farmers who were embarrassed were able to meet their liabilities and pull themselves through. Since the law has been in force, there seems to be a microbe or epidemic which has taken a few of those people, who have assigned at the instance of other people who are not so scrupulous as they ought to be. For instance some of the trustees go out into the rural districts and impress upon those people what the relief is under the law; that they ought to apply it to themselves, and that if they would put their affairs into the hands of the trustees, those trustees would settle all their difficulties for them. Under the old law, they had the relief of borrowing money on good terms in those rural districts where such facilities exist. On account of this new bankruptcy law, the people are afraid to do business with them, because they fear they may be left in the dark.

speechtext: What was the law in Quebec as regards bankruptcy? Is there no act by w-hich a resident of Quebec can voluntarily assign?

speechtext:
We have, under the law of Quebec, as I quoted before, articles 853 to 892, whereby a firm or a person who is a trader under his own name or firm name, could make a judicial abandonment of his property or be forced to assign where he owed morp than 8200. Then we had for in-
Bankruptcy

corporafed companies the .provisions general to the Dominion of Canada of the Winding-up Act.

subsubtopic: PROPOSED ABROGATION OR AMENDMENT OF BANKRUPTCY ACT, 1919
speechtext:
My hon. friend has given
figures of five or six years. I think he gave the figure of assignments in Quebec in 1921, as 2,451. Were those all assignments of merchants?

subsubtopic: PROPOSED ABROGATION OR AMENDMENT OF BANKRUPTCY ACT, 1919
speechtext:
I am not in a position to answer that question, but I may say that in a great number of these cases the people voluntarily assigned, which goes to show that under the new law they are more eager to seek relief, for the reason that they can obtain their freedom more easily than was formerly possible. Under the old law they were liberated only to the extent that their estate could pay; now they are fully liberated, under the provisions of articles 58 to 60, if their estate can bring fifty cents in the dollar. Under these circumstances they are more eager to seek relief, and that is why since 1919 up to the present time we have seen a great many more insolvency cases and bankrupt estates in the province of Quebec than we have known before.
When one sees all these insolvency cases occurring and so many bankrupts seeking relief, one is reminded of the old custom that prevailed in France, where conditions are of course different to-day. In the old days in France the insolvent was forced to wear a green bonnet until such time as all his debts had been discharged to the satisfaction of his creditors. But when we see how easily debtors can now have their affairs settled, and with what little trouble they can get out of their difficulties, I think that in a few years we may have to establish a new order of decoration. These people are so successful in escaping from their responsibilities that, I am led to believe, we may deem it advisable to give them titles. The principal difficulty of the new law seems to lie in the facility- greater than under the law as it previously stood-with which a man can obtain relief from the consequences of failure, and the greater ability he has now to free himself. As I pointed out a moment ago, this condition induces a great many people to seek relief, and is also a strong incentive to dishonesty, because I am fairly certain that a great many of these people must arrange with the trustees and some of the largest creditors before being able to settle their affairs as satisfactorily as they seem to be able to do.
The present state of things also undermines credit, because people are afraid to advance money to any tradesman for the reason that they fear he may fail and then be able to {Mr. Casgrain.l
avail himself of the provisions of the law at any time. Another objection to the law as it stands is the fact that the costs of liquidation are much too high. The law was intended to make all legislation uniform, but in my opinion, as things stand now, it only tends to make the evil uniform. I would also point out that this law encroaches on our provincial law, on our civil code and procedure. And one of the last, but by no means the least serious, of the objections I have to it is that it has been responsible for the appointment of too many trustees. When the law was first enacted we were given to understand that only about fifty trustees would be appointed for the district and city of Montreal, and that there would be some trustees located in other districts. I am told that in Montreal there are over 165, indeed, nearly 200 trustees to-day. Nearly everybody . could be appointed a trustee under this system, but at present I understand that the gates have been closed and that it is not so easy to have trustees appointed. Very good reasons must be advanced and more security given. The trustees under this law are supposed to give a bond in regard to their administration, but I am informed that many of them give no bond except when they have in view the settlement of an estate. When that is the case they go and give the bond.
As I said before, it has been pointed out that in some of the big cities a few persons have been acting as trustees notwithstanding that they have availed themselves of the provisions of the Bankruptcy Act and are themselves under compromise. In this respect I would suggest that the government adopt the course that was followed last year by the provincial government of our province. It was discovered that, in the case of a number of persons who were acting as commissioners of the superior court, there were certain abuses in some districts. The government discharged them all by process of an act which was passed at the last session, and only those were reappointed who could show that they were sufficiently qualified for the position. I believe that it would be well to-day if all trustees were removed by this government and if only those were reappointed who could give the best guarantee and recommendation. At any rate, I would not appoint as many as have been appointed in the past. All these men have to earn their living, and this is one of the reasons why we have seen so many of them going into the rural districts and inducing people to avail themselves of the law.

subsubtopic: PROPOSED ABROGATION OR AMENDMENT OF BANKRUPTCY ACT, 1919
speechtext:
Are they appointed by the Civil Service Commission?

Bankruptcy

subsubtopic: PROPOSED ABROGATION OR AMENDMENT OF BANKRUPTCY ACT, 1919
speechtext:
No, they are not under the Civil Service Commission, their appointment lies only with the Minister of Justice and the Secretary of State. Trustees are appointed by order in council. That is good.
It is my opinion that the bankruptcy law, with its many amendments and rules and regulations, is altogether too voluminous and complicated. We have a law that covers 72 pages and is embraced in 98 articles, and rules and regulations and every year since its , enactment it has been amended. Indeed, it was amended even before it was put into force, because after the act had been passed in this Chamber it was discovered, upon consultation with some of the best lawyers, that it contained serious errors and omissions. The amendments that have been passed, together with the regulations and forms, are very cumbersome and complicated, and the law consequently does not afford that measure of relief which the people had expected. The forms which it is required to comply with are also for the most part useless and costly, and I venture the opinion that the rules of procedure contain too much red tape, so that creditors will never realize their wish of seeing estates wound up with any degree of expedition unless these rules and regulations are made somewhat more practicable.
I might refer to another feature of the law. I am told that last year certain amendments were enacted by which a trustee is bound to make a return of the affairs of the insolvent debtor for the last year and the year previous to the insolvency. In most cases this has worked very unsatisfactorily both from the point of view of the trustee and, as well, from that of the creditors, more especially of privileged creditors. In one case of which I have personal knowledge a trustee had prepared all his dividend sheets and he received a notification from the Income Tax department not to pay any privileged creditors or any others before the Income Tax office had adjudged what amount was to be paid by the trustee on account of the returns not made and the taxes not paid by the insolvent debtor, depriving thereby the privileged creditors, as well as the lawyers, the trustee and other persons similarly interested in the estate of the payment of their just claims and fees. And in most of these cases, from the books that are kept by the insolvent debtor, it is absolutely impossible for the trustees to prepare such returns.
When we consult the statutes we find that not only once has this parliament tried to legislate in the matter of bankruptcy. But each time it has been unlucky. We find that
in 1839 a Bankruptcy Act was passed, only to be repealed in 1843, and six years later replaced by another statute. In 1863 Sir John Abbott introduced a bankruptcy bill which became law in 1864 and was amended from time to time. In 1874 under the Mackenzie administration a further bankruptcy bill was enacted, but six years later it was repealed. Judge Fortin, who later became a judge of the superior court of the district of Montreal, when a member of this House introduced a bill applicable to bankruptcy proceedings throughout the Dominion. With the assistance of some of the ablest lawyers of Montreal he drafted what it was hoped would bring relief to both debtors and creditors but the government of the day did not view the measure favourably, having in mind the unsatisfactory results obtained under the old law, and the bill failed to pass the House of Commons.
If we examine the defects of our old bankruptcy laws we shall find them practically the same as those which mar the Bankruptcy Act of 1919. On this point I wish to quote the views of Judge Desire Girouard contained in a book which he published on the bankruptcy law qf 1864. He then advanced the following objections to that statute:
Firstly, it is prejudicial to commerce, because it opens new doors to fraud, affords to the bankrupt new means of deception. What is to be expected from a law which, from the first to the thirteenth clause, and from the first to the hundred and thirty-first paragraph, favours almost always the insolvent and not the creditor? Be it remarked, this assertion is not gratuitous ; had we no other proof of it than the fact of all the advertisements and notices of failures, which have crowded, since the coming into force of the statute, the columns of our newspapers, our position would be fully established. But again, when we glance at the provisions of the act, the mode, voluntary as well as compulsory, of winding up the affairs of the insolvent ; when it is observed that the bankrupt has himself the control of the important delays of the announcement of his failure and the divesting himself of his estate; that he can still with impunity defeat the law and defraud his creditors, obtain, in spite of the latter, a judicial discharge; when it is clear that the hope of such discharge will be for the debtor a powerful motive to induce him to dimmish his assets, and afterwards to declare himself in a state of bankruptcy, in order to come out of it enriched with the spoils of the mass; when, we say, we consider all these complications and formalities, which here, as always, serve the debtor and not the creditor; when we remember, in fine, all these delays and costs of liquidation, without forgetting the expenses of the insolvent in obtaining his discharge and attending the meetings of creditors, for the arrangement of his own affairs, it is easy to see, we say again, that the fact, the evidence of which we invoked, it but the rigorous consequence of the law, the inevitable result of the provisions . of the act.
But it is not only because the act favours the interests of the insolvent to the detriment of his creditors that it is fatal to the commerce of the country, but because, like every other bankrupt law, it will injure our credit abroad.
Bankruptcy

And in support of his argument he quotes the following article from the Revue de Legislation written expressly for the benefit of Canada in 1846 when the bankruptcy law of 1843 was in operation:
"The internal commerce of the country," says the anonymous writer, "ought to be sober, prudent and limited; the bankrupt laws in assuring beforehand the discharge from debts, will render it improvident, hazardous, and rash; first cause of mistrust. The facility of freeing himself from embarrassments and of avoiding his struggle always uncertain, will on the very first difficulty paralyze the energy and determination of the trader; for why struggle to pay debts, when it is so easy not to have any? This is a second cause of mistrust. When the labour and talents of the insolvent were the settled guarantee of his creditors, it was for their interest to make this labour and these talents available: and thence all these aids and encouragements which never failed to the unfortunate, and which assisted him to overcome difficulties and to regain lost ground. Bankrupt laws have put an end to this state of things, and hence a third source of mistrust.'
Finally, we think we do not stretch the truth in affirming that a large number of merchants, if not the greater number, would be satisfied with few amendments and simple additions to the existing laws, for the sole purpose of defining and punishing fraud and giving to the cession de biens its proper and necessary effects.
I do not believe, Mr. Speaker, that either in the province of Quebec or in the Dominion generally do we need such a law as we find in the Bankruptcy Act of 1919. It is veiy hard to frame a law which shall be satisafctory of application in a new country, and we find that it was not until 1886 and 1898 that England and the United States respectively, both much older countries than ours, considered such a course necessary or desirable. We are a country in the making, and we have bo many new elements mixing with our population, so many foreign immigrants who are not educated to our standard of ethics and morality, and our territory is so vast, that it is very difficult to draft a general law of bank-rupcy to protect the opposing interests of creditors and. debtors and ensure a just and economical distribution of insolvent estates. If in the province of Quebec the resentment against the Bankruptcy Act is stronger than in other provinces, it may be due to the fact that, especially in the district of Montreal, we have a very large proportion of foreigners who sometimes are inclined to seek freedom from their indebtedness in a way that our native population would not consider for a moment. I am told that in the province of Ontario this law has not been so adversely criticised. The reason for this may be that there is one-third less population of foreign origin in Ontario than there is in the province of Quebec, particularly in the city of Montreal.

Under this law a further objectionable feature is that large credit corporations are enabled to wield too much influence. For instance, we see big corporations such as the Credit Business Men's Association and other trustee companies engaging in the liquidation of insolvent estates more than was the case under the old law. I do not say that this state of affairs is altogether bad, but I do Bay that these companies having better means of administering the estates of insolvents it is very difficult for individual trustees whc , are not so well organized to secure a fai [DOT] share of business, and this may be the reason why so many of these men go into outlying districts and try to induce people to assign.
Our present bankruptcy law has for the most part proven a boon and a benefit to the foreign element who have recently come to this country from Europe. They arrive here with neither a business nor any other reputation to lose and have no scruples about adopting questionable practices to rid themselves of their financial obligations.
The Bankruptcy Act of 1919 was introduced to secure a more equitable, speedy and economical distribution of a debtor's property and to prevent the excessive abuses and endless expenses which attend bankruptcy proceedings under the old system. But I believe the act was conceived in a hurry and was ill digested. In fact, it was one of those laws wished on us, like the Board of Commerce and other legislation passed by the Union government. which we later found encroached upon the rights of Quebec and the other provinces.
It saw the light, I am informed, in an obscure law office in Winnipeg, was fostered here by the hon. member for George Etienne Cartier (Mr. Jacobs) and finally adopted by the government of the day in despair. It has proved like our other bankruptcy acts, anti-social and anti-economic. It has done bo much harm and so little good that I submit it ought to be consigned to the pigeon-hole to take its place with the Board of Commerce Act and other defunct laws passed by the Union government.
The old Winding-up Act and the provisions respecting the abandonment of property in our code of civil procedure in Quebec are, I submit, sufficient to meet all present purposes and to give general satisfaction to the public. A few amendments may be necessary, but that being done I think everybody would be satisfied. Above all, what we need in a law of this kind, if it has come to stay, is plain and simple language, not the equivocal language which predominates

Bankruptcy
in the present act and which is the cause of much trouble and difficulty. It has been found under this law that in many cases the rights given to the province of Quebec under the civil code and the code of procedure had to be maintained before the courts through the submission of proof that notwithstanding this federal act we had the right to avail ourselves of certain provisions existing in our own laws. A gentleman who was in his lifetime a great lawyer in Montreal, Mr. C. H. Stephens, expressed the view that the code of procedure and the provisions respecting the judicial abandonment of property that we had in the province of Quebec were sufficient to meet all the needs of the people of that province. Speaking of the impossibility of removing from the minds of the people of certain provinces the idea that it is unjust and cruel to take the assets of a debtor and not liberate him from his liabilities, he said:
To expose the groundlessness of this idea, it ought perhaps to be sufficient to point out that for 15 years, this province has, so far at least as its local interests are concerned, got on better with the half a dozen articles inserted in our Code of Procedure, than under the most elaborate of the insolvent acts which were previously in force.
He pointed out that under our provincial law, a system for distributing insolvent estates, there has been less litigation, less costs and a total absence of that demoralizing influence which constituted the great predominating evil of the acts passed before the present law came into force.
I believe the remarks I have made are sufficient to show that the laws of this parliament in the matter of bankruptcy have not met with favour of the public at large. These laws were introduced with the idea of remedying the existing evils, but in each case it has been found after a few years of operation of the law that the best results were not being obtained. In fact, these bankruptcy laws have been a nuisance; they have been the source of much trouble in our province, and we have been forced to spend large sums to ensure the maintenance of our rights under the civil code and the code of civil procedure. I would also point out that when we had no bankruptcy act we got along just as well as, if not better than, we do under the present system.
Let us see what some of the best legal minds in the province of Quebec have to say about this law. There was a debate in the legislative assembly last year and the previous year, when a resolution was adopted in this form:
"The legislature of the province of Quebec regret that the Bankruptcy Act as amended invites dishonesty
and fraud and causes serious trouble to both trade and industrjr, which is of a nature to ruin credit, and it requests the federal government to repeal the act."
Hon. Mr. Perrault, Minister of Lands and Colonization for the province of Quebec, speaking in a debate last year, stated that the law had only opened the door to fraud and speculation; that it should not be amended but should be repealed. Hon. Mr. Galipeault, provincial Minister of Public Works, speaking on the occasion of the opening of the courts in the city of Quebec in September last, stated:
"The Canadian Bar, it is said, was responsible for the adoption of the new Bankruptcy Act by endorsing it after this project had been before the federal House for some time. If this is true, the association might have been more fortunate in its first move. The province of Quebec, which had the advantage of having its own bankruptcy law, which was less expensive and more easily operated will not be the only one to suffer from a law so rapidly studied, and which is so defective and means spoliation in many cases.
"For all those who are attached to our civil laws, constant care and watch is necessary to prevent any encroachment on our privileges.
"The tendency to centralize and unify legislation is becoming more and more visible since a few years, and there seems to be an admitted attempt to encroach on provincial rights and attack our civil laws.
The present Minister of Justice (Sir Lomer Gouin) expressed the same opinion a few years ago in addressing a convention of the Canadian Bar Association at the Ritz-Carlton in Montreal. He expressed the hope that when they recommended amendments to the different legislatures and to the federal parliament they should not ask for uniformity of laws which would be prejudicial to the laws of the province of Quebec. Hon. L. A. Tasch-ereau, Premier of Quebec, has also expressed his opinion with regard to the present law. I shall have to quote it in French, because I have the extract of his speech from reports published in the French newlspapers. Mr. Taschereau said:
The government has sanctioned the repeal of the act, Mr. Taschereau said, and now we shall have it examined by our most eminent legal authorities, and, should it be found to be ultra vires, we shall ask to have it referred to the Supreme Court so as to have it declared unconstitutional. The government think that the act has not proved satisfactory and it is willing to do its utmost so as to have it declared unconstitutional.
If bankrupts occur in rural districts, further states the Prime Minister, it is neither due to taxes, nor to the erecting of schools and building of roads, but evidently to the Bankruptcy Act. The rural country was deluged with soliciting agents who induced the farmers to go into bankruptcy and many were taken in. The Act has been disastrous to the credit of farmers and as long as it exists we shall find the same results which, at present, we are encountering. The Premier reiterates that the government will take all the means possible to have this unjust law repealed.
With reference to the maintaining of our rights under the civil code and the code of
Bankruptcy

procedure in our province, a case was decided last fall before the court of appeal, a case in which the Riordon Company was interested, the Danford case. A certain creditor claimed the right to exercise a certain privilege; the question was taken before the court of appeal, and in rendering their decision the judges said:
The legislators during the short period of life of the act have so amended it that it is scarcely recognizable in its present form. It may be that before the Supreme Court could pass upon the question, further amendments would be made, either making clear what is evidently ambiguous or destroying entirely all rights of the privileged creditor.
That is the judgment of the court of King's Bench. I am told that the question is now before the Supreme Court of Canada, but judgment has not yet been rendered. We have also, Mr. Speaker, not an expression of opinion, but some remarks made by the hon. Minister of Justice (Sir Lomer Gouin) himself when he had occasion to speak last year at a meeting of the Canadian Manufacturers' Association. At that time one gentleman made a speech regarding the weak points of the law and the difficulties occasioned by it, and this is what the Minister of Justice is reported as saying. on that occasion-I quote in French:
I cannot but thank, said Sir Lomer Gouin, Mr. Deslongchamps for his interesting remarks on the Bankruptcy Act. I had already heard complaints in regard to this legislation, but this is the first time I have listened to such a clear statement of the grievances with which you have to put up. I am aware that bankruptcy laws have been adopted by the government, and some provinces, and, I also know that some have been repealed when they were found impracticable. I cannot express an opinion on what has been said by Mr. Deslongchamps, but what I may say without hesitation, is that manufacturers for whom this act was passed have made representation to the government that the act lends itself to abuse and that it is not in the interest of trade and the community at large, and, they may rest assured that the government will do its duty and give them justice.
On another occasion we have the report of Mr. Lambert, who was the president of La Chambre de Commerce of Montreal, who was reported as having had an interview also and discussing these matters with the Minister of Justice. I will read the following clipping with regard to the interview:
He also reported on an interview accorded himself and other members of the chambre de commerce by Hon. Sir Lomer Gouin, when the bankruptcy law had been discussed. Eleven amendments, recently approved by the Chambre had been submitted to the Minister of Justice and Sir Lomer Gouin had told them that he would do all in his power to see that a drastic change would be made as soon as possible. He had gone further, continued Mr. Lambert for he had declared that if the law was not repealed it would undoubtedly disappear anyhow, as it had been found most unsatisfactory for everybody concerned.

I have here amendments submitted by La Chambre de Commerce of Montreal, which are eleven in all. I think the Minister of Justice must have had copies of these amendments because I believe they were submitted to the government. They point out certain modifications which would likely be made, in order to improve the present law, if it is not repealed, along the lines I have suggested this afternoon. I will not weary the House reading these amendments, or reading different letters which I have received from numerous manufacturers, industrial and other people in my district in the province of Quebec. I am glad to know we have at the head of the Department of Justice the minister who now occupies that position (Sir Lomer Gouin). He was leader in the province of Quebec for many years, has made good laws a,nd brought prosperity to the province. I admit that this law might have some good effects, but it was not satisfactory on all points, and needs amendments, if amendments can possibly be made. If too many amendments would render the law ambiguous, as pointed out in the judgment of the court of appeal, I think it better to repeal the law entirely, and get the best legal minds in this country, those who have had the best experience, to frame up a new law which would give satisfaction to the province of Quebec and to the Dominion at large.
On the other hand, if the law is to remain as it stands, and if we have not time this session or other sessions to enact a new law, it might be provided that this law should not apply in the province of Quebec. A few years ago we had a law similar, which was of widespread application, the Lord's Day Act, but when that act was passed a provision was made that every province in the Dominion which would pass a similar law, or which had a law in existence before the passing of that act, would be exempted from the operation of that Dominion law. I want to see the rights of the province of Quebec protected, and I would like to see our civil code and civil procedure maintained in integrity.
I hope the Minister of Justice will do his best to remedy the present existing conditions as regards the province of Quebec.

subsubtopic: PROPOSED ABROGATION OR AMENDMENT OF BANKRUPTCY ACT, 1919
speechtext:
As one of those who had something to do with the Bankruptcy Act now under discussion, when that act was passed through this House two or three years ago, perhaps it would not be out of place for me to offer a few remarks in regard to the motion now before the House. It so happened that I

Bankruptcy
had the honour of occupying the office of Solicitor General of Canada at the time when the Bankruptcy Act in its initial stages came before parliament. I believe in the first instance my hon. friend for George Etienne Cartier (Mr. Jacobs) introduced the bill into this House; that bill was subsequently taken over by the government as a government measure and entrusted to myself as its manager in its course through parliament, and in that way I became fairly familiar with the provisions of the act and with its general application. I do not know, from the wording of the present motion, whether it is the desire of my hon. friend who has brought this matter to the attention of the House whether in his opinion the act should be actually repealed, or merely amended. There is a great difference between the two proposals. I submit to my hon. friend that the principle of a uniform bankruptcy law for the Dominion of Canada is a proper principle. It is possible, and it is also probable, that many of the details of the present act might well be amended, but I submit that we in Canada should have one uniform bankruptcy law to be applicable throughout the whole Dominion of Canada. What was the position in Canada prior to the passage of this act. We had nine provinces in Canada, each having provincial legislation which was virtually bankruptcy legislation although the several provincial governments had no constitutional power to pass such laws, they came as close to the constitutional limit as it was possible for them to come in their respective provinces, and in the nine provinces of Canada these laws exhibited very great variety and entirely lacked uniformity. There was great difficulty in finding out just what the law of this, that or the other province was. The House will agree that trade and commerce is essentially a national question, just as much a national question as our railways, or our banking v system. It is just as important to have a law pertaining to our trade and commerce uniform in regard to bankruptcy as it is to have uniformity in regard to railway law or in regard to the laws of banking and commerce. One difficulty arose almost from day to day by reason of the large amount of interprovincial trade that is done in this country. The difficulty was this. A man in Nova Scotia sold goods to a man in Manitoba, the man in Manitoba became unable to pay for his goods; and the question was, what was the man in Nova Scotia to do to cbllect his bill? He did not know the Manitoba law, it might differ very materially from the law of Nova Scotia. The same thing might happen
in regard to British Columbia, Saskatchewan, Alberta or Ontario, because the laws of all these provinces varied, and in some instances varied very materially. There was no uniformity, and there was a vast amount of uncertainty and of ignorance in regard to the exact situation even in our country. What about the foreign trade of the Dominion? We were doing an enormous trade with the United States and with Great Britain and with a great many other countries and it happened that of all the civilized trading countries in the world Canada and China were the only two that did not have a modem and uniform bankruptcy law. Complaints came to Canada from time to time from representative commercial bodies of other countries, from representatives of boards of trade and chambers of commerce in other countries, as well as from exporters of goods from other countries to Canada complaining of the unsatisfactory state of the bankruptcy law of this country. Foreign firms were in some instances averse to extending mercantile credit to Canadian merchants by reason of the uncertainty which prevailed in regard to bankruptcy legislation in Canada.
The only legislative authority in Canada having constitutional power to pass a bankruptcy law is the Dominion parliament. This is settled by the express terms of the British North America Act. And the question arose whether this parliament should attempt to remedy the difficulty and pass a uniform law in regard to bankruptcy and insolvency throughout the whole Dominion, or whether we should permit nine attempts to create bankruptcy legislation in the various' provinces of the Dominion none of which had any strict constitutional right to pass such enactments. Parliament took the view that it was proper to have a uniform law upon the subject. The framers of the British North America Act in 1867 thought the Dominion parliament was the proper legislative body to deal with such a question, and power was given expressly to this parliament to do so. This parliament in 1875 passed such an act. That act was only in operation in Canada some five or six years at the most and then, in the judgment of parliament, it was repealed. It was held that the administration of that act had not proved satisfactory; and if one will read the debates in parliament at that time he will see that the chief complaint against the administration of the act of 1875 was the charge that the trustees or, as they called them in those days, the official assignees in insolvency, were incompetent men. also that they were irresponsible men, that.
1.502
Bankruptcy

time and time again the estates of a debtor had gone into the hands of an assignee and that was the last heard of it-the assignee through himself and his friends, managed to eat up the whole of the estate; there was nothing left for the creditors. That was the chief ground of complaint against the act of 1875. The act was repealed. We had no bankruptcy act in Canada from the year 1880 down to the year 19J9 when the present act was passed.
The bill which became the act of 1919 was introduced into parliament in the year previous. A special committee of this House, upon which sat representatives from every province of the Dominion, worked, and worked diligently, upon this whole question. Twenty-four meetings of that committee were held; I had the honour of presiding over the committee and I know whereof I speak. We worked long and we worked late, and at the end of the session we were able to bring in a bill which was in the nature of a draft measure. In order that parliament and the country might have time to digest it, the bill was only allowed to go to its second reading. An enormous number of extra copies of the bill were ordered to be printed so that they might be circulated from one end of the Dominion to the other. Copies of the bill were sent to all the provincial legislatures, to the law officers of the Crown in all the provinces of Canada, to all the mercantile bodies of standing in the Dominion, to all the boards of trade, all the chambers of commerce, all the legal associations, to the banking associations, to labour organizations, to the wholesale apd retail associations of traders; and I may tell the House likewise that representatives of nearly all of these bodies appeared before the committee and submitted their views, and I do not remember that any single individual, or any body of individuals, offered any objection to the principle of the bill- that is, that we should have a uniform Bankruptcy Act in Canada. Of course we differed -differed very radically from time to time- as to many of the clauses of the bill. In 1919 the bill again came before parliament. During that session the legislation was threshed out in this House clause by clause, item bjr item. Amendment after amendment was offered, and amendment after amendment was accepted. The desire of parliament was to secure the best bill and the most uniform bill that it was possible to secure in order to meet the varying conditions throughout the Dominion without infringing more than was absolutely necessary upon the local enactments of any one of the provinces. We considered that we had been able to report a
EMr. Guthrie.]	*
fair and reasonable measure under all the circumstances-not by any means a perfect measure; no one dreamed that a perfect measure could be produced in either a year, or two years, or three, or four, or live years, and so experience has shown since the act was passed. Imperfections have developed from time to time. In Great Britain the bankruptcy act is frequently amended. So also in the United States, and I assume also in the countries of Europe wffiere they have had. bankruptcy legislation for generations back. I do not believe that any great measure of general application can be passed at a session of this House and remain as a perfect model of legislation for any number of years to come; it will have to be
5 p.m. amended and altered from time to time. I find that during the last twenty odd years the Dominion Lands Act has been amended, I think every year; the Railway Act has been amended almost from year to year. Not so with the Banking Act, because we revise that every ten years; but I believe the present Bankruptcy Act will have to be altered from time to time for the next one hundred or the next one hundred and fifty years; it will have to be amended to meet changing requirements, the changes in our conditions, and the changes in our methods of trade.
Now, if my hon. friend who introduced this motion desires to get any concrete results from it, what I submit to him is this:	He
should bring in his proposals in the nature of a bill to amend the act. He has gone over the act from end to end; he has criticized it here, criticized it there, and criticized it in the other place; but he has left us no. concrete proposal as to its amendment. If he would merely come before parliament-perhaps he could not this session but at any rate next session->
with a bill to amend the act in the various sections concerning which he seeks amendment then the House, I think, will be in the position to discuss the question intelligently. But I am satisfied from what I know of the bill, from what I know of the temper of the House and the views of hon. members, that the House will agree, by a large majority, that the principle of the legislation is good and should be maintained. Although the details of the act may require a large amount of amendment to make it more workable there is this to be noted, that outside of the province of Quebec I do not think there has been any serious objection raised to the act itself. We had the advantage of advice from the province of Quebec with respect to this act, when it was before the committee in 1919. We had the assistance of the Bar Association;

Bankruptcy
and many eminent and well known men from that province also advised the committee upon various questions. We had resolutions from chambers of commerce and boards of trade in the province of Quebec as well as from all the other provinces, and the committee endeavoured as best it could to put the ideas of those experience! bodies and able legal minds into legal form in the various sections of the act as they now appear upon the statute book. I have heard considerable criticism regarding the administration of this act in the province of Quebec, the criticism that my. hon. friend has voiced to-day-that there are too many trustees in that province. I heard it stated within a few hours-not by my hon. friend but by another hon. member of this House-that there are ever 170 trustees in the Quebec district alone-

speechtext:
In the city of Montreal alone. Well, that is far beyond what anyone expected when the act was passed. We took particular pains in regard to the question of the appointment of trustees. We thought we safeguarded that branch of the act pretty well. We provided that no man should be appointed a trustee unless he possessed qualifications which would fit him for the office. In addition to that he was bound, in the first instance, to give a bond for $10,000 before he was appointed at all. In the next place there are provisions which safeguard the estate and creditors and compel the trustee to give bonds for every dollar that goes into his hands. These were clauses which were added in view of the experience which we had under the act of 1875; and the main idea was that only outstanding, capable, qualified men, who could give this security would be appointed to this office of trustee, as well as trust companies which had been incorporated in Canada for the purpose among other tilings of acting as trustees in the case of insolvent estates. I was amazed to-day to hear that there are some 170 or 165 trustees in the Montreal district alone. I was under the impression that if there were twenty-five or thirty that number would be quite sufficient to do the whole business of that district and do it well.
It has been intimated by the mover of this resolution that in the province of Quebec abuses have sprung up in the matter of fees on the part of trustees and also of the legal profession. If this is true it is in direct contravention of the provisions of the act-	[DOT]

And some one should be brought to account. That act prescribes what trustees and lawyers may take lawfully.
