subsubtopic: PROPOSED ABROGATION OR AMENDMENT OF BANKRUPTCY ACT, 1919
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, when the Bankruptcy Act was introduced in 1919, I believe I was the only member of this House to protest against the passing of euch legislation. My protest at that time was based on five main reasons. The first was because I thought it would open the door to fraud and dishonesty. The second one because I was of opinion that it would disorganize trade and commerce. My third reason was because
Bankruptcy

the law was made applicable to nontraders, and I thought at the time' it was bad legislation to apply a law of bankruptcy to non-traders. My fourth reason was because it was an infringement on civil rights. And my last reason was that I was afraid that the government would practically destroy the benefits of the law by appointing political partisans as trustees.
The experience we have had with this law for two years and a half confirms the fears that I expressed at that time in the House. The law has been in force for a little over two years. Parliament has already made ninety-two alterations; complaints are coming from all parts of the country, and for the same reasons as I gave in 1919 against the adoption of the law, I support the resolution of the hon. member for Charlevoix-Montmor-ency (Mr. Casgrain). I do not say that I would go as far as to repeal the law in its entirety. If the other provinces of confederation are willing to keep the law in the statutes, let them keep it. We have had on our statute books and we still have a law existing from 1880, or over forty years, a law on abandonment of property, a law which has been tested and which has been found to be a good law. It has been practically abolished by the federal Bankruptcy Act. We want to go back to that law. There is no necessity for uniformity in a bankruptcy law. The hon. member for South Wellington (Mr. Guthrie) who spoke before me stated that he was in favour of the principle of a uniform bankruptcy law, but I did not hear him give any good reason for that. The reasons he gave were that we needed a law that would be applicable in all the provinces, so that merchants in any province would know what kind of law existed throughout Canada, and they could reach their creditors. If his reasoning was good, we should say that most civil laws should be the same in all the provinces. Why? The civil laws are very close to trade and commerce. Trade and commerce is within the purview of the federal government, I will admit; but most civil laws are applicable to trade and commerce in every province, and when for instance a trader or a merchant in Vancouver or in Winnipeg sells to or buys from a merchant in Montreal, he is under the civil laws of Quebec as regards his sale or his purchase. If uniformity of the law is a matter which is absolutely desirable, we should make it applicable, not only to the bankruptcy law, but to all the laws

subsubtopic: PROPOSED ABROGATION OR AMENDMENT OF BANKRUPTCY ACT, 1919
speechtext: The framers of our constitution boldly stated and enacted that bankruptcy should be applicable to the whole Dominion, and they gave this parliament the only power to deal with the subject.

subsubtopic: PROPOSED ABROGATION OR AMENDMENT OF BANKRUPTCY ACT, 1919
speechtext: That may be true; but my hon. friend will also admit that under section 92, subsection 13 of the British North America Act, civil rights are within the purview of the provinces. My hon. friend will also admit that in enacting a bankruptcy act, he can scarcely avoid touching on civil rights.

subsubtopic: PROPOSED ABROGATION OR AMENDMENT OF BANKRUPTCY ACT, 1919
speechtext: That is right.

subsubtopic: PROPOSED ABROGATION OR AMENDMENT OF BANKRUPTCY ACT, 1919
speechtext: I believe I can show to the House that many of our civil laws have been touched and altered by the Bankruptcy Act.

subsubtopic: PROPOSED ABROGATION OR AMENDMENT OF BANKRUPTCY ACT, 1919
speechtext: Does the hon. member not know that under the British North America Act the provincial authority has no right at all to legislate on bankruptcy?

subsubtopic: PROPOSED ABROGATION OR AMENDMENT OF BANKRUPTCY ACT, 1919
speechtext:
That may be true in principle; but the act has been on our statutes for forty years, and if it had been such an infringement of the British North America Act, I am sure the matter would have been raised before. The law has been on our statute books since 1880, and the question has never been raised. The reason why it was never raised was because bankruptcy matters were too close to civil laws and civil rights.
The hon. member for South Wellington also stated that, with the exception of China and Canada, there was no country in the world which did not have a uniform bankruptcy act. My hon. friend will admit that in all those countries, if there is a uniform Bankruptcy Act, it does not apply to nontraders. Outside of Canada, there are in the world only two countries at the present time, where a bankruptcy act applies to nontraders, and those countries are Britain and the United States. In France, Belgium, and all the other countries of the world, there is a certain bankruptcy law which is not at all dissimilar to ours; but it does not apply to nontraders. It. is illogical to apply a bankruptcy law to non-traders for whom credit is not essential. My hon. friend (Mr. Guthrie) also stated that the chief complaint against the law of 1875 was that the assignees, who are now called the trustees, were charging too much, and that therefore the law was abrogated. We have the same complaint to-day. I have in mind a case in which the total assets payable to the creditors amounted to $700 while the costs came to $1,600. My hon. friend went on to say that there was no complaint

Bankruptcy
outside Quebec, which was the only province whence there came any word against the Bankruptcy Act. I might read to the hon. gentleman what Mr. Detchon, the manager of the Canadian Credit Men's Association, has to say on this subject. He is the gentleman whom I may call the power behind the throne, the one who inspired the member for George Etienne Cartier (Mr. Jacobs) and my hon. friend for South Wellington (Mr. Guthrie). Speaking in Winnipeg on October 4, this gentleman stated, as reported in the Montreal Gazette of that date:
The law as it exists at present is on the side of piracy, it is claimed, by the men who have been close to its operation, and the manoeuvres of a portion of the trading community who have been quick and sharp to take advantage of its weakness. Where one class of the retail trading community can buy in their own stocks at fifty cents on the dollar or less, it is extremely difficult for the efficient, honest trader to continue to compete with any fair degree of success.
" Gentlemen, take 45 cents on long term payment or you get nothing," is the word passed by the wholesale traders in many instances. Along with the report on a long list of cases it is pointed out that 9 per cent of the men reported on have bought fine residences, run high-priced motor cars, and many keep their families at the beaches for the summer.
This complaint does not come from the province of Quebec; it comes from the manager of the Credit Men's Association, who lives, I believe, in Winnipeg, and who, practically speaking, is the father of this legislation. After having studied the act and the way in which it has operated, he finds just what I have quoted him as having said. The other comment offered by my hon. friend for South Wellington was that there were too many trustees. He told the House that he did not know that there were as many as 145 or 130 trustees in the city of Montreal, and added that during his administration good care had been taken to name as trustees only men who were reputable. Well, I have here a return to an order of the House dated April 26, 1921. I had asked this question:
What are the names of the trustees under the Bankruptcy Act for the district of Montreal? When were they appointed, and what were their respective occupations before their appointment?
In reply to this question I find, to my amazement, especially after the statement of the hon. member for South Wellington, that from July 6, 1920, to December 26, 1921, the old administration had appointed in the district of Montreal alone 118 trustees. I do not believe, therefore, that my hon. friend's statement, that he thought there should be only 25 trustees and that we should take good care to name only men of good reputation, is worth very much.

subsubtopic: PROPOSED ABROGATION OR AMENDMENT OF BANKRUPTCY ACT, 1919
speechtext: Does my hon. friend know of any case where an application was refused when the applicant was prepared to put up a bond of $10,000?

subsubtopic: PROPOSED ABROGATION OR AMENDMENT OF BANKRUPTCY ACT, 1919
speechtext: No, I did not inquire into that; I did not investigate. But the fact remains that we have the statement of the hon. member for South Wellington that 25 trustees would be sufficient for the district of Montreal, and as opposed to this we have the proof that during the administration of the late government, of which he was a member, they named 118 trustees for that district.

subsubtopic: PROPOSED ABROGATION OR AMENDMENT OF BANKRUPTCY ACT, 1919
speechtext: What is the objection to the appointment of any number of trustees so long as they qualify under the provisions of the act? Is there any more objection to that than there would be to the appointment of a large number of justices of the peace?

subsubtopic: PROPOSED ABROGATION OR AMENDMENT OF BANKRUPTCY ACT, 1919
speechtext:
Yes, there is an objection, because there should not be too many trustees appointed to take care of a limited amount of business. It is obvious that if there were sufficient business for five or ten trustees, say, and you appointed only that number, they would not try to obtain all sorts of business; by all means they would not go after people and try to make them assign. The state of affairs in the province of Quebec, whatever it may be in any other province-and I do not know that it is not the same-is simply amazing and outrageous. The other day a reputable lawyer of Montreal, Mr. Calder, in an address before a business men's association on the Bankruptcy Act, produced partnership agreement which he showed to his audience and the last paragraph of which read as follows:
In case of bankruptcy profits will be divided equally.
I could bring before the House many typical cases, and especially one in the district of Montreal, where the trustee went after a certain person in a rural district against whom there was a judgment. The trustee wrote this man a letter and in reply the gentleman came to Montreal to his office. The trustee told him that he knew the person who had the judgment against him and that he could probably make a settlement or obtain a certain delay for the payment of the debt or the satisfaction of the judgment. Here the party who came to the trustee was not a very well educated person, he was ignorant of the law and was under the impression that this trustee was really trying his best to get a settlement for him with that creditor. The trustee inquired into the man's busi-
Bankruptcy

ness, and after getting from him a list of his creditors he requested him to sign a paper authorizing him, the trustee, to interview the principal creditor who had taken judgment. A few weeks later the man found that he had signed a demand in bankruptcy and that a petition had been made on that demand.

subsubtopic: PROPOSED ABROGATION OR AMENDMENT OF BANKRUPTCY ACT, 1919
speechtext:
Was the assignor in that
case actually insolvent? If so there was no great harm done.

subsubtopic: PROPOSED ABROGATION OR AMENDMENT OF BANKRUPTCY ACT, 1919
speechtext: No. But even if he was insolvent I submit that harm was done him.

subsubtopic: PROPOSED ABROGATION OR AMENDMENT OF BANKRUPTCY ACT, 1919
speechtext: Was the so-called trustee prosecuted under the criminal code?

subsubtopic: PROPOSED ABROGATION OR AMENDMENT OF BANKRUPTCY ACT, 1919
speechtext:
The case is pending in court. I will read to my hon. friend the letter which the man received. This is .a translation of it:
Dear Sir,-At the present moment we are going through a very difficult crisis and we find that a great many business men who have been in business a number of years are forced to make certain compromises with their creditors in order to maintain their business. Probably you, as do many of your confreres, need somebody to settle your affairs with your creditors. Do not be afraid to come and see us. If you want to maintain your trade at its maximum and to also maintain your previous standing, you have to avoid failure or bankruptcy. We are making a specialty of arrangements of all sorts between creditors and debtors. If the matter interests you, you can come and see me, or I will come and see you myself and give you a full explanation regarding this proposal.
Well, naturally this man, having done his best to obtain some delay from his principal creditor and having failed, was delighted to receive such a letter. He went over to that party, who was not a trustee, and was directed by him to the trustee, but he was always under the impression that the trustee who spoke to him was the party who had written the letter. He went over and, as I related before, he was made to sign a demand of abandonment. A petition was made by the court, and a few Weeks later a meeting of his creditors was called. I may say that this man came to see me and told me his story, and I directed him to another lawyer. This lawyer made a contestation, which is now pending in court. No doubt criminal proceedings could be taken, but I do not think it would be wise to do so before judgment is delivered on the case in the civil court.
My hon. friend for Charlevoix-Montmo-rency (Mr. Casgrain) has covered the ground pretty well and there remains little further to be added so I will shorten the remarks I had intended to make. He stressed a point which in my opinion is very important. Under the Quebec law, as he stated, which we had for

forty years, a debtor could never get his discharge. He was allowed to resume business after settling with his creditors for 50 or 75 per cent, but the creditors could take a judgment for the whole amount of their debts and collect if they desired to do so. The result was that after having made a compromise with his creditors, if on a second venture he made money these creditors could collect the balance owing them. But the present law is a direct encouragement to gambling. The merchant or manufacturer takes all kinds of chances, he may indulge in the wildest speculation, but he need not care if he does not make good, because under this bankruptcy law he can settle with his creditors for 40 or 50 per cent and start all over again, as many times as he likes.
My hon. friend for Charlevoix-Montmo-rency has also mentioned the various clauses in our Bankruptcy Act which infringe on the Quebec act. As I stated in my opening remarks, I do not contend that this parliament has no power to legislate on bankruptcy, but I do submit that when the law of bankruptcy is so closely related to civil rights, the Dominion parliament should be very chary about legislating in this matter. For instance, we had our old law governing the relations between lessor and lessee. Under the Bankruptcy Act the lessor has practically no protection when his lessee becomes bankrupt; all he is entitled to is three months' rent due. The trustee can take over the store, sublet it to a third party, even if there is a clause forbidding same in the lease, and the lessor has simply to acquiesce in the action of the trustee. Under the old act of Quebec, the fact of a lessee becoming bankrupt or abandoning his property automatically cancelled his lease, and the lessor was entitled to twelve months' rent due, if it was in arrears for that length of time; he was entitled further to damages for four months where the failure occurred four months before the expiration of the year, and to damages for twelve months if not.
As I said before, it may not be necessary to abrogate the law in its entirety. If the other provinces are satisfied with it, we have no objection to their taking that view. But as I have pointed out, for forty years we have had a very complete law, a law that has been tested and found good. The present federal law was passed upon the demand of the western provinces, and I believe it should be amended at least in such manner that it will not be applicable to the province of Quebec.

subsubtopic: PROPOSED ABROGATION OR AMENDMENT OF BANKRUPTCY ACT, 1919
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I think the importance of this resolution demands the attention of all hon.

Bankruptcy
members of the House. The proposal is double-barrelled in its character; it asks for an amendment and it alternatively asks for abrogation. It is apparent from the remarks of the proposer (Mr. Casgrain) that he desires that the law should be abrogated.
It is not my intention to repeat any of the arguments or observations that have been made by previous speakers, but I may say that from the point of view of the people of British Columbia-and I believe the same idea prevails very largely in the prairie provinces-we are much better off with the Bankruptcy Act than we would be without it. The purpose of the act, as I understand it, is not to enable debtors to go through crooked forms of liquidation, but to preserve the assets of crooked debtors for the benefit of honest creditors who have lent them money or given them credit on goods. In just cases the law is such that through the courts and the ordinary administration of justice it is possible to enable perfectly honest debtors who, through unforeseen circumstances or other causes entirely beyond their control, have got into difficulties, to obtain a discharge from the courts and to start afresh with a new hope and a new opportunity, whereas the old law made the debtor under such circumstances a slave to his creditors and his community and the victim of unforeseen or unwise acts. Not only does the bankruptcy law preserve the assets for the creditors and ensure a larger measure of justice to the debtor, but I believe it is the best method of liquidating the estate of a debtor at the least possible cost. Then again, the bankruptcy law maintains uniformity and makes for stability in trade and commerce.
That the present law needs amendment is apparent to any lawyer who has had practice under it. But what have we as an alternative? As hon. members seeking to discharge the responsibility of legislators and not catering to whims or to votes-and we do not do such things-I suggest, Mr. Speaker, that if you abrogate the bankruptcy law you revert to the legislation which is still on the statute books in many provinces. I will take the case of British Columbia, because I am familiar with that province, and I would ask hon. members who are interested in this bankruptcy law to give attention to the remarks which I will make with respect to conditions prevailing before the Bankruptcy Act came into force. In British Columbia, if	a man found himself
in serious financial difficulties, three courses were open to him. He might sit down and allow his judgment creditors to rush in and sell him out, with others tumbling
after as fast as they could. Or if it were a company, it would go into voluntary or involuntary liquidation under the Companies Act. Or if it were an individual, he might take advantage of the Creditors and Trustees Act whereby he would assign all his goods, all his property real and personal, to a trustee, who would handle them for the benefit of the creditors. The result was that men who took charge of estates were often in league with the debtor, were often not competent, not honest, not qualified. to handle the assets. Then, the expense was great; the fees foi liquidation and for legal services ran into enormous sums. I cite to the House the case of the Dominion Trust Company, with which many hon. members may be familiar, in which in one year, I believe, the law fees-not for litigation, but merely in connection with the liquidation of the estate-ran up to $28,000 or $30,000.
Under these old provincial acts we also have uncertainty so far as the position of the debtor is concerned. He could never be discharged from his liability; even if he were an extremely honest man he may have been confronted, as sometimes occurs in the lumber business, with an unforeseen and unpreventable disaster-for instance, a fire sweeping his timber areas and destroying everything he possesses from the business point of view. He puts himself in the hands of his [DOT] creditors being obliged to do so from no fault of his own. What is his position? He is condemned for life so far as his activity in the business community is concerned; he can never get on his feet except behind the skirts of his wife or under the guise of an incorporated company. And even then he would not be safe, he has a hopeless future. Now, the purpose of the bankruptcy law was to give the honest man who is the victim of circumstances an opportunity to commence his business life over again.
The hon. member who proposes this resolution drew attention to certain abuses in connection with it whereby it was made easy for a man to avoid his obligations; whereby trustees facilitated liquidations under the Bankruptcy Act with the result that there were crooked and dishonest transactions. Well, my contention is that that would happen no matter what law you put into force in connection with bankruptcy. Where men are willing to be dishonest, where they have no respect for their character or their reputation and will employ crooked methods, then the law does not count for very much, unless it be the criminal law,-and it will be found that in the Criminal Code the attempt at

Bankruptcy

fraud to the advantage of the perpetrator, either as affecting money or credit, is amply covered. So that really, so far as the principle of the law is concerned, the contention of the hon. member that the act enables people to do crooked things is hardly a good argument, because they will carry out dishonest actions in other ways.
Now, Mr. Speaker, I believe this resolution should be rejected by the House, first because the resolution is confusing. If you adopt it, you make it possible for the law to be broken. I think the suggestion of the former Solicitor General, the member for South Wellington (Mr. Guthrie) is a good one, that a measure of this kind, to be dealt with intelligently by the House, should be handled by the hon. member bringing in his amendment in specific form, so that we may know exactly with what we are confronted. If we are to vote on the principle of doing away with the Bankruptcy Act or not doing away with it, I suggest to hon. members, apart from the reasons I have given, that they look in their own constituencies and see whether or not the business, the industrial and commercial interests of. those constituencies, or the responsible people of those constituencies who are interested in the business of the district, are asking for the repeal of this act. I do not think there are many portions of Canada where you will find that such a feeling exists, and where there are difficulties existing, I believe Mr. Speaker they can be overcome by an amendement and not by a complete abrogation of the law.

subsubtopic: PROPOSED ABROGATION OR AMENDMENT OF BANKRUPTCY ACT, 1919
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise with pleasure to support the resolution of the hon member for Charlevoix-Montmorency (Mr. Casgrain). Indeed, as aforesaid, the bankruptcy act of 1919 and its amendments do not give to the people of our country the expected results, that they constitute a source of complaints on behalf of industry and trade, and that, at last, it is desirable to abrogate them or, at least, to greatly modify them. Before starting to study certain principles, the principal basis of this law, Mr. Speaker, let us glance over the judiciary administration, with regard to its laws and its connections with trade and industry, during the epoch that has preceded the year 1919. A bankruptcy law existed in each province of confederation. Creditors and debtors recovered in the proceedings as ordered by the provincial courts of justice. These local bankruptcy laws have been carefully studied, amended when required, by the provincial legislators and were giving, indeed, legal satisfaction. Moreover, this legislation had been enacted according to provincial

necessities and customs, further resembling, as much as possible, the remaining laws in force in such and such a province. On the other hand, we had the Winding-up Act applying to the whole Dominion of Canada with regard to incorporate trading companies in liquidation. Everything appeared provided for and then we believed the legislators were very wise. The creditors, always dissatisfied when becoming connected with a bankruptcy, accepted their lot without bad grace in virtue of the dividend sheet prepared by the curator or the liquidator. We, for example, in the province of Quebec, were satisfied on our part. The confusion in which we are at present confirms the past and obliges us to prefer our former situation. Our law, called "Assignment", comprising articles 853 and following, of the Quebec Civil Code of Procedure, was excellent. Any unlucky trader found justice, and the community found efficient protection. We remember, Mr. Speaker, the day when a proclamation of the Governor General, dated December 31, 1919, announced to the Canadian citizens that the Bankruptcy Act, to-day in force, and of which as enacted, we complain bitterly, would come into force on and after the first of July, 1920.
Now, Mr. Speaker, if we examine this act, it is interesting to remark that, from the first of July, 1920, to June 28th, 1922, it has suffered eighty-seven amendments. In fact, it was born before its time, and its numerous amendments have served it as an incubator. And, after all, how could it be otherwise? For, constructing a bankruptcy act for the whole Dominion, without consulting the provincial attorneys-general and the legislatures directly interested in the approval and the application of this law that superseded a bankruptcy system already established in every province, was an extremely difficult move. As an experimental act, it has embraced too much. Its construction has been badly calculated, and it has had need of many braces. It now approaches three years since that law was brought into force. During this period has it given the expected results? Together with the interests of trade, of industry, with the chambers of commerce and the public in general, we do not hesitate to answer in the negative. It has disturbed the commercial population of city and country. It encourages neglect and the breach of honest and frank commercial customs. It has diminished the urban and rural credit. It contributes, finally, as applied or tolerated, to the lowering of the honesty and morality of some individuals. The blindfold partisans of the Bankruptcy Act would answer: "But the principle of the

Bankruptcy
law is good; it was asked for in 1919 by various commercial institutions of the different provinces, we will remedy the abuses shown to exist. We will amend the act so as to satisfy any just claims which may be advanced by the public."
Very well, Mr. Speaker, let the act remain in our statutes, if such is the desire of the majority of the members of this House and also of this government, in which I place my trust, but, let us receive, without further delay, the wishes of the commercial and industrial world who have for more than two years watched carefully the exploitation of this unfortunate act, and suffered its disastrous effects, and this, nowithstanding the after-war crisis through which we have just been passing. Therefore, I say, let us amend the act during the present session.
The abuses come from the disposition of the act itself giving an opening to all kinds of modern procedures. It has been abused enormously, Mr. Speaker. A change is needed to reinstate confidence and good faith, on the whole, in all bankruptcy matters. And we will reach that end by applying [DOT] this act only to the tradesman who has ceased his payments, In the interest of the agricultural class, it is not convenient and it is unnatural that by the general law the farmer should fall under the operation of this act.
We understand that the tradesman has some risks to face. A reduction in price takes him by surprise and the effect on his business is such that he is sometimes thrown on the street. The war suddenly stopped-happily for the nation; the immediate result for the tradesman was, for example, the collapse of prices in silks, woollens, lumber and many other articles from sixty-five to seventy-five per cent. By its very nature, trade is very often risky in peace just as in war, in spite of the good name and the capital of a well-established firm. This is why a bankruptcy act is necessary to trade.
On the other hand, the farmer-and I am speaking now of the real cultivator of the field who has farmed from generation to generation, who likes his work and acquires experience with each succeeding harvest-is established permanently. Although he encounters some risk, although he has to face bad weather, he is almost never completely wiped out.

subsubtopic: PROPOSED ABROGATION OR AMENDMENT OF BANKRUPTCY ACT, 1919
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, continuing my remarks, I would add that this act, in offering to the agriculturist the opportunity of assigning, is a barrier to agriculture, hindering realization of the ideals of attachment to the land, annulling the effort of the farmer to balance his budget. The attraction of the city is then very bright. The farmer has no longer the same credit at the bank; discount is often refused to him. Even those who habitually lend money on farm property dare not lend to the farmers. Since these last have the right to assign, a privilege which they sometimes use, lenders prefer to buy debentures or shares in incorporated companies, more or less good, from salesmen who invade their neighbourhood. To-day, many people prefer a scrap of green paper, nicely engraved, to the value of a farm. This is how the act is at present affecting the solvency of the farmer.
Anyone who has studied our Bankruptcy Act will agree that it is a commercial tragedy. It brings on the scene five actors who play the principal parts. These are the assignee, the authorized trustee, the creditors, the registrar and the judge. As a finale, by way of apotheosis, when the curtain falls, there is the discharge, the rehabilitation in business. We have listened, Mr. Speaker, since July, 1920, to daily representations of this tragedy throughout Canada. We are now entirely justified in asking its withdrawal or, at least, in making necessary amendments, erasing certain sections which give rise to abuses respecting trade and the general public.
What are amongst thousands, the outstanding grievances against this act? First, the assignee ought to be a recognized tradesman; he should make his assignment in the district in which he is doing business, and in the hands of one of the trustees appointed for that district. Thus the creditors would have knowledge of the failure at its beginning, and trustee and assignee would be carefully watched during their work. Too much facility of procedure in bankruptcy is to be avoided It is surprising to note that, according to the present law, the province of Quebec-and the same is true as regards the sister provinces
forms only one district in bankruptcy matters. Any person doing business and residing at Montreal can, as he sees fit, assign at Montreal, or at Quebec, or at any other centre in the province. Really, this fact is laughable. The petition should contain the honest assent of a serious creditor, and it
1510
Bankruptcy

should not be returned except after notice has been given to the assignee. To-day the trustee always finds reasons which he judges sufficient to return the petition without notice. This manner of procedure must stop for the advantage of everyone. Moreover, under the old law, the tradesman must have kept a cash book; or otherwise, no discharge was granted. We should oblige business people to keep books according to the usages and customs of commerce. The title and privileges of trustee should be conferred only on those who are really competent. A deposit of $2,000 to the federal treasury could be required from each trustee when nominated, as a guarantee of good faith, and this, in addition to the ordinary security exacted by the said act.
The business of bankruptcy, Mr. Speaker, is, in these times, very lucrative for the trustees. We are informed by creditable persons, sometimes the victims of these fakirs, that there exists a type of bankruptcy beggar who annoys honest people who have no intention of assigning, under the pretext of advantageously liquidating their stock. A federal inspector should be appointed to supervise the operations of trustees and to examine their books. The trustees, most of the time, do not have their bills of costs taxed. This inspector would see to this matter. Each province should be allowed to formulate a table of costs and supervise its just application. If the trustee so desires, according to the law, he may have a bankruptcy sale of immovables by the sheriff of the district in which the said immovables are situated. But he is not obliged to do so. He may also sell them himself after proper notice. It is needless to add that this is the usual manner of procedure. The sheriff's sale is a notable exception. In the future, an amendment made to the act would oblige all immovables to be sold by the sheriff. In any event, the sale of immovables by the trustee should be made only after the permission of the judge has been obtained. In addition, the trustee should tell the judge why the sale is necessary.
In the application of this act, two trustees often quarrel over the possession of a bankruptcy stock. It is delightful, Mr. Speaker. We should avoid these morbid discussions by leaving to the first trustee in possession the right to look after the bankruptcy stock until such time as it shall be otherwise ordered by the judge. Besides, the nomination of a crown prosecutor to supervise the bankruptcy cases and the filing of claims, sometimes false and simulated by shady creditors, would do good work towards the cleaning. The discharge would not be so easily obtained, for the increase of claims is beneficial to those

who ask the discharge. To this effect, services are rendered to the assignee at the expense of oath. Fraud would then be punished by justice in the name of the state and at its expense, because fraud punished at the cost of the individual is never punished. It is the duty of the state to be directly interested, and France gives an example to many other nations on this point. The registrar, in my humble opinion, has too much power. He refers to the judge only contested cases. All procedures, after the assignment, should be presented to the judge to be ordered as law. What an enormous amount of dishonest proceedings would thus be avoided, discovered and rejected. This would be a protection for the actual creditors who are nearly always victimized by the tortuous procedures allowed under this act.
This act is based on English law'; precedents form the law. In Canada, the act of 1919 gives an absolute discretion to the judge. The matter depends on him; it is the absolutism of the judge. For instance, who decides on the discharge offered by the assignee? The judge alone. It is not the act itself which decides or prescribes the .procedure. No positive law text exists on this subject. This is a grave oversight which must necessarily be remedied. If an amendment is passed in regard to the manner of obtaining, and the requirements for discharge according to principles established and stated, judges themselves charged with the administration of the present law would be very well pleased, because the law as at present constituted gives them too great a responsibility. The immovable foundation of states, says the Greek poet Pindar, is justice. The grievances of the industrial and commercial world against the Bankruptcy Act are undoubtedly true and receivable in law as in fact. This cause is just; and when a cause is just, it must sooner or later triumph. I am assured, Mr. Speaker, that it shall triumph.

subsubtopic: PROPOSED ABROGATION OR AMENDMENT OF BANKRUPTCY ACT, 1919
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I unreservedly approve the resolution of the hon. member for Charlevoix (Mr Casgrain), and I deem it my duty to rise in this House so as to further give him my full support. The question brought up by the hon. member is one of the most important subjects that have been debated during the present session and I hope that the House will give it their most serious consideration, which it really deserves. It purports to a law which affects the financial interests of a large number of people in this country, and the application of which has up to now given the most fatal and disastrous results.

Bankruptcy
Mr. Speaker, the principle of the Act is defective and unjust, because it aims to limit, restrict, even to do away entirely with obligations legitimately contracted. To my mind, I have always considered and more than ever do I now believe that the legislator exceeds his powers, when he adopts legislation having for effect to liberate the debtor from his debt without having entirely discharged it. There is but one person who can remit a debt and that is the creditor. It is his privilege, his right, and any parliament which, through legislation, foils the creditors of that right, abuses its powers and is guilty of a denial of justice. I am therefore opposed, as a matter of principle, to all bankruptcy laws, and I think that the late government was ill advised in enacting the one of 1919. If I may judge from the protests which arise a little everywhere, and especially in my province, against the pernicious effects of this act to every point of view, I think it should be immediately struck off the statutes of Canada. I shall not, however, venture as far as to ask for its repeal, but I am strongly of the opinion, and, my own personal experience convinces me every day the more, that it should be radically amended.
The Bankruptcy Act as understood and applied fosters dishonesty. I will go further. I shall add that it is unjust inasmuch as it protects especially the debtor, to the detriment of the creditor which it leaves at the mercy of numerous annoying and costly procedures which, in practice, prove illusive. I contend that a bankruptcy act should have for its aim to protect first the creditors, and that the right to instigate bankruptcy should exclusively belong to them. I am therefore especially opposed to section 9 of the act which allows every person without any discrimination, whose debts are over $500, to make, of his own accord, an assignment of his property to the benefit of his creditors. This section makes no exception. Everybody is permitted to make an assignment of his property; the professional man, the artisan, the farmer, the ordinary beggar-as it has already happened-may avail themselves of the provisions of this section. It only requires to be indebted to the amount of $500 or more.
I represent a rural county, Mr. Speaker, and, I am proud to say, it is one of the finest counties in the province of Quebec. In my riding there are no large industries, nor any powerful business corporations, but fertile farms dotted here and there with beautiful villages where simple virtue survives, and I believe that the principal grievance we have to make against the Bankruptcy Act comes
from the section just cited. I have not the slightest doubt that if members of this House were aware of the working of this Act in rural counties, they would without hesitation amend it in such a way as to comply with the aim the legislator had in mind when it was enacted. My knowledge is based on experience. I have seen this law in operation in my district and I am sure of not exaggerating when I say that it is most depressing and demoralizing. Not only is it harmful to those who wish to take advantage of it, but it is especially injurious to the farming class whose credit it ruins, and there is a general hue and cry against what is known almost everywhere, pardon the expression, Mr. Speaker, the "damn" Bankruptcy Act.
Who are the culprits? First, I have no hesitation in pointing out the trustees of bankrupts. I am aware that there are conscientious, competent and honest trustees, but they are in the minority. I sympathize with the latter and do not refer to them. I am alluding to the majority who, lacking the virtues or qualities that I have just mentioned, do not take into account that the trustees are appointed to apply the law but they imagine and end by really believing that the Bankruptcy Act is administered for their benefit. It then becomes a race, an organized campaign in search of victims to sacrifice on the altar of authorized assignment. The trustees are on the look out day and night; they have recruiting agents and the moment they have an inkling of a person seeming somewhat financially embarrassed, they find means of meeting their intended victim, having him interviewed, proposing all kinds of schemes, verbally assign him so to speak and finally convince their victim that he had better make a clean slate of it and begin life anew, and wipe out all obligations contracted up to date. The debtor first listens, then on the spur of the moment or feeling somewhat depressed gives in, allows himself to be convinced and signs an authorized assignment. His creditors did not demand an immediate payment, they were willing to give him time; but not being consulted in the matter, they learn of the accomplished fact through a notice of the trustees requesting their presence at a meeting. In most cases, the debtor regrets his haste; he would be differently disposed a few days or even a few hours after, but the thing is done, the winding-up follows its course, the debtor's property is sacrificed, the creditors receive a year or two later a dividend of 10 or 20 per cent, when there would have been enough to settle in full with them, and the trustees who. in most cases, hardly earned

Bankruptcy
previously, $1,000 or $1,500 per year, now are in receipt of cabinet ministers' salaries.
Does this description, Mr. Speaker, seem too much exaggerated? It is not. It is the true narration of the application of the Bankruptcy Act in the rural country, at least in my district and the neighbouring ones.
In my own village I came across the following case: A certain person signed an authorized assignment under the same circumstances that I have just mentioned, the transaction had hardly taken place when the person discovers his mistake; two hours later he arrives at the trustee's home to inform him that he had changed his mind, and, would he be kind enough to return the assignment. After a long discussion over the matter, the trustee consents, demanding, however, an indemnity of $200. Was it to recoup himself for the work done? No, it was to indemnify himself for the fees he would lose if this assignment was not carried out. I can name the person in question. The trustee is still in office. I intend to ask for his dismissal and I hope that it will not be refused.
Is this, Sir, an isolated case? I contend that it is not. Cases of this kind are numerous; it is the general rule. On three different occasions, when the assets of the bankrupt comprised only a property mortgaged to its full value and that the inspectors had authorized an assignment in favour of the last creditor, subject to said mortgage, I was witness to trustees demanding in advance fees amounting to $400 and $500, simply for his signature in connection with the assignment. Still there are more glaring instances. In another village of my county, a merchant, immediately after the Bankruptcy Act came into force, took advantage of it to request a composition which was granted to him, and, naturally, it is almost the invariable rule in the composition that it is followed up by an authorized assignment. The latter was not yet settled when he again made-this happened only a few months ago-another assignment and this with the same trustee. Four long years under the rule of the Bankruptcy Act. Consequences: the merchant in question has just left the village without a cent to his name. The trustee is now the registered owner of both the property and trade of the bankrupt which he is disposing of, and, I am not aware that the creditors have received a cent.
It may be said that the act provides for such abuses as I have just mentioned. In theory perhaps, but in practice it is but a. disillusion. How is it possible for a creditor interested in ten, fifteen or twenty bankruptcies, to be present at all the meetings, follow the procedure, protect himself before the
fMr. Boucher.]
courts and thereby incur considerable expenses. It is not done and not possible. The trustees and the debtor are practically the masters of the situation, and the creditor has to be contented with what is handed to him, and he may consider himself lucky if he receives anything.
By keeping track of the nature of transactions which, as a rule, take place in rural districts, I am convinced that the Bankruptcy Act will be found to be the cause of serious prejudices to creditors without being of any benefit to debtors, for the simple reason that in 80 per cent of the cases, without taking into consideration the considerable charges that the trustees demand, the debtor could pay 100 per cent in the dollar if a judicious winding-up was carried out.
I think, Mr. Speaker, that the abuses that I have just mentioned would greatly be reduced if all of Part II of the Act were repealed.
The highest authorities in my province have denounced this legislation, men whose names I mention in this House with a certain pride and admiration, and moreover, I feel certain of meeting the unanimous approbation of the House in saying that they are amongst those who incarnate what is most noble and best in the French-Canadian race. The Hon. Alexander Taschereau, Premier of the province of Quebec, and the Hon. J. B. Perrault, Minister of Colonization, have in the course of the last session, at the Legislative Assembly, condemned this act in the clearest possible way, and in my estimation their word is authority on such matter.
Somebody suggested exempting the province of Quebec from the application of the Bankruptcy Act. This is the best solution and I would welcome with pleasure an amendment to that effect. Up to this day the people of Quebec have been noted for their loyalty, honesty and integrity. They wish to remain loyal to their traditions and in no way do they want to be legally exempted from paying their debts. Should it not be possible to adopt this amendment, I think it would be to the purpose and beneficial to amend the Bankruptcy Act as follows :
1.	That Part II of the act be so amended that the authorized assignment and the composition will no further apply;
2.	That the Bankruptcy Act be only ap-jlicable to trade as in the act of 1875;
3.	That the scale of fees of trustees be more clearly defined;
4.	That trustees' fees be only levied on the proceeds of the sale of movables and that the immovables contribute to the extent of

Bankruptcy
the costs only of sale and awarding of moneys resulting from said sale;
5.	That a penalty be imposed upon trustees who, directly or indirectly, induce a person to go into bankruptcy, divide their fees or split a commission.
I do not state, Mr. Speaker, that all is defective in the present act. I am willing to admit that in certain spheres and in special cases its existence is warranted and may be useful, but I think it is capable of being amended and that these amendments impose themselves to answer to the needs of those who I have the honour to represent in this House, these fellow citizens with whom I am proud to share both their ideals and aspirations.

subsubtopic: PROPOSED ABROGATION OR AMENDMENT OF BANKRUPTCY ACT, 1919
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the resolution contemplates two things: First the abrogation of the Bankruptcy Act; second, its amendment. From what I have heard so far I would not think there is any intention, even on the part of those favouring the resolution, that the act itself should be abrogated, but rather that certain amendments should be made thereto.
There seems to be a difference between the law in the province of Quebec and that in the province of Ontario prior to the passage of the Bankruptcy Act of 1919. If I understood aright what has been said, in the province of Quebec, farmers, for instance, were not entitled to the benefit of the Assignment Act -I am not giving it its proper name under the Quebec Code. I would point out to my hon. friends from that province that in Ontario farmers have always been entitled to the benefit of our Assignment Act. Its door was not closed to anyone in financial difficulties. At any time prior to the passing of the Bankruptcy Act anyone could make a voluntary assignment for the benefit of his creditors, and the same results were obtained as under the present act, with the one outstanding difference relating to discharge.
So far I find four main objections are made to the act. The first is that it is not confined to traders and merchants as in Quebec; second, that it was born too soon; third, that assignee's costs and fees are excessive; and, fourth, that there should not be a discharge.
Why anyone should want to withold the provisions of this act from a farmer I cannot see. Happily we do not as a rule, in the province of Ontario at all events, have assignments by many farmers. But if a farmer should get into financial difficulties why should not he be entitled to make an assignment under this act just as well as anyone else, be he merchant or otherwise. On behalf of the TMr. Boucher.]
farmers-and I regret to say that during the hard times of the last two years there have been in my own county to my knowledge four or five assignments by farmers-I am glad to think they can avail themselves of the provisions of this act and giving a proper account, of their dealings with their estate and satisfying the other provisions of the act get their discharge and start off again with a clean sheet and with a new lease of business life. Under our former act this was not the case. If a man failed, and his creditors wanted to pursue him, he was up against it. The only way he could start business again was by trading in the name of a fake company or in the name of his wife.
I think it was my hon. friend from West-mount (Mr. Mercier) who said that this practically was an eight months' child-that it was born too soon, because there were too many amendments. I happen to have in my hand the Statutes of 1921 and I observe that our criminal code contains for that year twenty-four amendments-about half as many as this act. The criminal code has been the law of our land for many, many years, and if at this stage it is necessary to put through twenty-four amendments to this long established law, surely it is not going too far to put through twice as many amendments to new legislation.
In regard to assignee's costs and fees, I was very much struck by the case cited by the hon. member for Chambly and Vercheres (Mr. Archambault). The assets were only $600 and I think he said the assignee's fees were about $1,500 or $1,600. I am not sure whether I have repeated the figures correctly or not.

subsubtopic: PROPOSED ABROGATION OR AMENDMENT OF BANKRUPTCY ACT, 1919
speechtext: The amount that remained to be distributed among the creditors was $700, and the fees were $1,600.

subsubtopic: PROPOSED ABROGATION OR AMENDMENT OF BANKRUPTCY ACT, 1919
speechtext: What were the gross receipts?

subsubtopic: PROPOSED ABROGATION OR AMENDMENT OF BANKRUPTCY ACT, 1919
speechtext: I could not tell my hon. friend.

subsubtopic: PROPOSED ABROGATION OR AMENDMENT OF BANKRUPTCY ACT, 1919
speechtext:
Of course, it is that feature which governs. In the case referred to there is ample remedy provided by the act. Under the section dealing with trustees' fees a trustee is limited to five per cent. Solicitor and counsel fees are governed by stringent provisions contained in section 67. If the estate referred to by my hon. friend amounted to only $600, the assignee's fees would be limited to $30 and the solicitor and counsel fees, even if they secured the unanimous consent required by the act, would be limited to ten per cent, or $60-a total, all told, of $90. If any assignee in the province of Quebec or his solicitor retained $1,600, or indeed any-
Bankruptcy

thing over $90, there is ample remedy under the act and it should have been invoked, and I cannot conceive of the creditors acquiescing in these excessive charges.

subsubtopic: PROPOSED ABROGATION OR AMENDMENT OF BANKRUPTCY ACT, 1919
speechtext: The amount included all expenses, advertising and so on.

subsubtopic: PROPOSED ABROGATION OR AMENDMENT OF BANKRUPTCY ACT, 1919
speechtext:
I am, of course, only dealing with the commission and fees. We must add to those the disbursements provided for by the act. I do not think any estate of $600 would involve disbursements of more than $75, or $100 at the outside. So this was a case of gross fraud, and I am at a loss to understand why the creditors interested did not take steps to protect themselves, for the act provides against any such extortion.
It was also argued that the act is prejudicial to the interest of creditors. I cannot see how it has that effect. Certainly it does not in Ontario, for beyond the question of discharge there is no difference between our previous law and this law. As I said before, anyone can assign and get the benefit of the act. The only difference is that under the former procedure he could not secure a discharge.
In regard to discharge let me deal with some of the provisions that have to be complied with. A bankrupt will not be entitled to his discharge unless his assets are sufficient to pay 50 cents on the dollar, except in the special circumstances referred to in the section; if he has failed to keep books of account he cannot get his discharge; if he has continued to trade after knowing himself to be insolvent, he cannot get his discharge; if he has failed to account satisfactorily for any loss or deficiency of his assets or to account for his liabilities, he cannot get his discharge; if he has contributed to his bankruptcy by rash and hazardous speculation he cannot get his discharge; if he has given any undue preference to his creditors, he cannot get a discharge; if he has made a previous assignment, he cannot get his discharge; and last, and perhaps most important of all, if he has been guilty of any fraud or fraudulent breach of trust, he cannot get his discharge. There are other provisions that I have not even read. When one views those provisions it is hard to see how any man who has not dealt fairly with his creditors, who has not been honest, can secure a discharge. If he has been honest and dealt fairly with his creditors, and through misfortune has failed, is there any member of this House who wants to see such a man go through the balance of his life as a debtor pursued by his creditors? Is it not better that when he shows he has acted honestly he should get his discharge and get off to a fresh start in

life? Those were, as far as I could see, the main objections to the act.
While I am on my feet I want to say a word or two regarding amendments. I have heard it suggested that the Minister of Justice is going to introduce a bill providing some further amendments to this act, and I certainly think there is room yet for amendments. I want to refer to one or two.
In the first place, the provisions regarding the preferential claim of a landlord for rent do not seem to me to be reasonable or fair. Under the Assignments and Preferences Act under which we formerly operated in Ontario, a landlord in case of failure, if he had been considerate of his tenant-who may have had a crop failure and the landlord may have given him an extension-if there was a year's rent in arrear and a failure took place, the landlord was given a preference for one year's rent immediately preceding the time of failure. Now it is limited to three months, so if a tenant wants an extension from his landlord and there is any danger, he cannot get it for the landlord would stand to lose at least nine months' rent, and the tenant suffers accordingly. That is not fair or proper. I cannot see why if a landlord is considerate enough to give his tenant time and the tenant has the misfortune to fail, the landlord's preference for at least one year, which was the law in Ontario before, should not still prevail.
Then, under the act he is only entitled to a preference for three months under the acceleration clause, and I would like to point out to the minister the effect that has. Suppose a farm lease is dated the 1st of March, rent not payable in advance, and a failure takes place say on the 1st of June. The landlord can secure three months' rent immediately preceding failure. If the assignee retains possession, the landlord, of course, can receive rent for whatever time possession is retained, but he can only secure three months' preference after the assignment. The crops are in the ground. He could not even get them. The most he could get would be six months' rent. The crops could be taken by the assignee and for the balance of the year, namely six months, the landlord would go without his rent, for a new lease would not be effective till the following spring. If there is any thought of introducing amendments, I would strongly urge on the minister a consideration of the section dealing with the preferential claim of the landlord, both for his protection, and that of the tenant.
There is another feature to which I would refer, and that is the powers of the -registrar. In the province of Ontario we have one regis-

Bankruptcy
trar. A failure might take place in lore William, yet practically everything you want to do in connection with the assignment has to be done in the city of Toronto where the registrar is. I am offering no criticism of the registrar at all. We have one of the most capable officers of the courts in Ontario as registrar, but I would suggest to the minister that there, should be some change there. Why we should not have our assignments registered and dealt with in the first instance in all ex parte applications-simple proceedings such as examinations and so on-in the office of the local registrar or local master in each county, just as is done in connection with supreme court proceedings, I cannot see. Where we have more difficult matters to deal with we have two judges to dispense the law. If you want even to examine the debtor, who might live in Windsor, or Kingston, or Fort William, the provision of the act requires the debtor to be examined in Toronto before the registrar. Surely that is not reasonable. I want to protest against the centralization of the operation of this act in one or two large cities in any province. Let us bring the provisions of this act as close to the door of the failure as possible, because the people interested in the failure are generally within that county. I am aware that in the case of merchants perhaps, most (freditors would be in Toronto or possibly Montreal, but outside of that this change that I suggest would lead to the convenience of the people interested. If there is any thought of amending the act I would therefore suggest that that feature be taken into consideration also.
For my part I heartily approve of the Bankruptcy Act, and would be very sorry indeed to see it abrogated. I do not fear that for a moment, but by all means let us get all the suggestions we can for its improvement, and in the end I have no doubt an act will be worked out which will be complete, which will be convenient, and which will be less costly than the proceedings required by the act at the present time, and will be just as fair to all concerned.

Mr. JACOBS; It may have been the hon. member for Charlevoix-Montmorency (Mr. Casgrain). I do not think everything that the Union government did was bad. In fact, I think the best thing they did was when they retired from the government of this country.

speechtext: The discussion this afternoon from this side of the House, and the essays which were so beautifully read by the members from the province of Quebec, would almost lead one to conclude that they were written in the office of the Nationalist sheet, Le Devoir. Le Devoir has always been opposed to this measure, and the reason they claim is, that it is an encroachment upon the civil rights of the people of the province of Quebec. -It is claimed by Le Devoir and its supporters that the Bankruptcy Act is an attempt on the part of the English-speaking people of the other provinces to impose upon the province of Quebec, English law; that this is the thin end of the wedge, and that before very long we may have the whole English body of law imposed upon the province of Quebec. That is frankly what is at the back of this agitation to repeal the Bankruptcy Act. I know whereof I speak, because I am a very diligent reader of Le Devoir. speechtext:
I have improved on account of it. I always like to know both sides of the question. I like to know what the other man is saying and what he is thinking. I have given the reason for the opposition to this law. If I thought that this Bankruptcy Act was the beginning of an attempt to impose English law on the province of Quebec, I would be the very first to oppose it, for the reason that if I know any law at all the only law I know' is the French civil law of the province of Quebec, and , if English law were imposed on that province I would be at a loss to know what to do, because I would have to go out of active practice. It is wrong for our people in the province of Quebec to say that the act which the parliament of Can-
Bankruptcy

ada has a right to impose on the whole of the Dominion of Canada is an attempt to take from the people of the province of Quebec their civil rights and their civil law. The British North America Act gives to the federal power the right to legislate in certain matters for the whole of the Dominion of Canada. The Bank Act, for instance, is a federal act, and the Merchant Shipping Act, the Criminal Code are also federal acts. Not only the present Bankruptcy Act but those that preceded it are federal acts. If the residents of the province of Quebec, or if the legislature or the lawmakers, or if the Fathers of Confederation from the province of Quebec, felt that a law of this kind would eventually mean that their law would be superseded by the law of the other provinces, why did they not in explicit terms say that these federal laws should not apply to Quebec? Here is a statement made by serious minded members of parliament, and eminent lawyers like my hon. friend for Chambly and Vercheres (Mr. Archambault) and my hon. friend for Charle-voilx-Montmorency (Mr. Casgrain), to the effect that this law should not be made to apply to the prpvince of Quebec. For my part I have this to say: that I would rather see the act completely repealed and abrogated than to have it apply only to provinces other than Quebec. This is something which the federal parliament has the right to impose, and so long as we have that right I say that we ought to exercise it, inasmuch as it is a measure for the general advantage and benefit of Canada.

subsubtopic: PROPOSED ABROGATION OR AMENDMENT OF BANKRUPTCY ACT, 1919
speechtext: What about prohibition?

speechtext: My hon. friend for Chambly and Vercheres (Mr. Archambault) always thinks in terms of prohibition. One would imagine that, with his visits to Montreal once or twice a week, he would be able to forget his troubles between those visits. What is the trouble with the Bankruptcy Act as shown by the discussion to-day? One is that the costs of the attorneys and trustees are extortionate, and another is that there are too many trustees. That is a matter which can be very easily changed by an ordinary amendment. I myself believe we have too many trustees. We have in Montreal about 150 trustees. Now 150 men cannot live in the city of Montreal on the business provided in that city or in the district of Montreal.

subsubtopic: PROPOSED ABROGATION OR AMENDMENT OF BANKRUPTCY ACT, 1919
speechtext: How many of those trustees were appointed at the request of my hon. friend?

speechtext: I will take the responsibility of saying that I suggested five or six to the Union government. speechtext: On what principle or reasoning would the hon. member limit the appointment of trustees, seeing that practically all the trustees engage in other business besides that of handling liquidation?

subsubtopic: PROPOSED ABROGATION OR AMENDMENT OF BANKRUPTCY ACT, 1919
speechtext:
I do not think they should be engaged in other businesses, but that they should give their entire attention to this work of insolvency. It is impossible for 150 men to live on the business provided in Montreal, and it is just possible that when a man cannot live honestly he perhaps resorts to other means. The complaint has been made that many of these trustees go about from place to place, particularly in the farming districts, and they seduce the righteous farmer from the path of virtue. It is an easy matter for the farmer to fall, they claim, particularly in the province of Quebec. I do not know why that should be, but it seems to me that the method has been resorted to. I say that no respectable trustee, or no man who deserves the name respectable, should resort to that sort of work. If we had fifteen or twenty proper trustees in Montreal, they would see to it that the law was properly observed, and if it were not properly observed the trustees would find themselves removed from office.
Now with regard to the question of these extortionate charges, hon. members who just preceded me referred to the statute but they did not refer to those sections which say explicitly that no trustee and no attorney shall receive more than 5 per cent of the proceeds of the estate. For the benefit of my predecessors who spoke on this resolution, and some of whom I am afraid have not even read the act, I would refer to sections 40 imd 67 of the act, which provides that no trustee or no attorney can charge more than 5 per cent. If they were restricted to that rate, I do not

Bankruptcy
think there would be any cause for complaint, and if the number of trustees were further restricted both these causes would be removed.
On the question of the unconstitutionality of the act, it is all very well for hon. members to rise in their seats and tell us that this act is unconstitutional. I would refer them to a number of privy council cases, where it was held that the Bank Act, the Bankruptcy Act and other federal acts which were deemed at one time to,conflict with provincial jurisdiction were found to be quite constitutional. It is not for this House to sit in judgment and declare whether the act is unconstitutional or not. If it is unconstitutional, or the House thinks it is, let the courts be applied to, and if the courts say it is unconstitutional, that is an end of the act. I know that Mr. Tasch-ereau, the Premier of the province of Quebec, lias declared that he will stake his reputation upon the uncorstitutionality of this act. Well, I Was very much surprised indeed to hear that statement made by the Premier of Quebec. He is one of the ablest lawyers in our province and a great constitutional authority, but I think when he made that statement he was talking more as the Premier of the province of Quebec than as a lawyer of the standing everyone knows he has reached.
A further complaint has been made against that act-not this afternoon, but I have seen it mentioned in the press and elsewhere-in regard to the loose way in which it is drafted. They claim the English in the act is not what it should be, that no person is able to understand it, and that it is so confusing that no one can make out its intent. All I can say in answer to that is, that this act is a replica of the English Bankruptcy Act passed about. 40 years ago, with its amendments. All of us who practice law know that there are no better draftsmen in the world than the English in matters of legislation, and if . these men who complain cannot understand what the real meaning of the act is, it is not the fault of the English in the act, but perhaps it is due entirely	to	themselves.	I know that oftenthere is difficulty in clearly understanding the meaning of a new statute, but it is only a question of time when these sections of the law will be interpreted by competent authority, the	judges on the	bench,	and in	duecourse the law will be as clear to them as it is to those who practise in England. This Act, I submit Mr. Speaker, ought to be given a chance.	It	has only	been	on the	statute books	about two	years	and a	half.
We cannot see yet how it is going to work out. If we find that there are abuses, later we may take steps either to repeal or to amend the act. At the present time, I submit, it should be given a chance to function, and those who are trying to administer it should be afforded the opportunity of giving it a fair show.
Another complaint that was made, was that the act is being amended all the time It is being amended, that is true, quite often, but for the purpose of improvement. The law must keep abreast of the advancing tide of public opinion. What may have been good three or four years ago may not be good to-day. We did not claim that this bill when it was draughted and submitted to the judiciary, when it was submitted to the trustees, to the trade and to others, was perfect, or that there were not certain defects in it when the measure was brought before the House. From time to time the law was amended and, as I said before, it was amended in order to improve it and not otherwise. I do not believe that the fact that the law has been amended is in itself a proof that that law is bad; the amendments made to it are for the purpose of improvement.
Now, my hon. friends who have spoken here to-day on this side have no concrete suggestion to make with regard to this act. They say that it is a vicious act and that it produces fraud; they say it is productive of dishonesty and consequently it ought to be abrogated. In what sense does this act induce fraud and dishonesty? Do my hon. friends know that there are about seventeen or eighteen sections of this act which deal particularly with fraud and dishonesty on the part of debtors; sections which practically cover every case of fraud and dishonesty. It may be that these are not invoked as much as they should be. I know what the tendency is in insolvency matters. When a bankruptcy takes place the desire of all the creditors is to get as much as they possibly can out of the wreck, which is only human, and instead of prosecuting a fraudulent debtor and sending him to prison, as perhaps they should do ethically, they are anxious to get what they can out of the estate, and that is why these people are not prosecuted. We have heard statements made here to-day by gentlemen who would seem to be acting more as attorneys for creditors, but we have not heard a single word about the debtor's side of the case. Surely the debtor has some rights also. The debtor says, when he has handed everything he owns in the wide world over to his creditors, when the estate is wound up and
Bankruptcy

he has nothing further-not even enough to start with again-because no privileges are given to the debtor-and no fraud of any kind can be charged against him, "I have a right to be given another show to start off again afresh." That is the theory of the act; but my hon. friends here say "No. Once a man has gone into insolvency he should be made to pay a hundred cents on the dollar, and until he does that he cannot go into business again." The rule of the old Roman law, was that the creditor should be able to ell his debtor into slavery. If a man is not able to start off afresh and earn a living for himself and his family, but is constantly in danger of being persecuted, by the creditors, then I say, we are lapsing back to the condition under the old Roman law, and our civilization of two thousand years amounts to nothing at all.
My hon. friends bn this side also say that we ought to go back to the provincial code of civil procedure, which is a law that worked for many years and worked harmoniously and successfully. Do my hon. friends not understand that under the British North America Act the provincial legislatures have no power whatever to pass any bankruptcy act; and the so-called Insolvency Act to which they refer simply consists of a scheme whereby the debtor's assets are disposed of by auction or tender and the proceeds distributed to the creditors. It is not a bankruptcy act at all; it is merely a scheme of division. The only authority that can deal with the question of bankruptcy is the parliament of Canada; and if we repeal this act then we go back to the old system whereby a man, as I said before, will have to remain under cover practically all his life unless he has satisfied his creditors to the extent of every penny that is due to them.
Now, in connection with the discharge of the debtor. My hon. friends, I trust, know that no discharge-no matter whether it is for fifty cents on the dollar or over-can be granted unless the judge examines carefully into the entire state of the debtor's affairs. My hon. friends say that this act induces fraud; that a debtor throws his assets into the hands of a. trustee; he obtains a settlement or a compromise and starts off afresh. That is not a fact. Every scheme of settlement, every scheme of arrangement or compromise must be submitted to the judge. Notice is given to every creditor who is interested to appear on a certain named day before the judge to show cause why this debtor should not be given his discharge. If any person appears before the judge and points out that some fraud mentioned in the act

has been committed-and there are scores of these mentioned in the act-then the judge must deny to the debtor the right to obtain his discharge. So that we have here a distinct division made between an honest debtor who obtains his discharge and the dishonest debtor who does not obtain his discharge. If this act were repealed or abrogated they are all thrown into the same category; the honest and the dishonest debtor are refused their discharge, and we are just, as we were before. I say, Mr. Speaker, we have now arrived at that stage in our national development where we want a bankruptcy act similar to those laws which they have in even-other country in the world.

Now, with regard to the question of the rights of the lessor, and other rights referred to in the Bankruptcy Act, which seem to have been changed from the law as it existed before the act came into force, I may say that the entire question is now before the courts to determine as to whether the parliament

of Canada has the right to interefere with the lessor's claim against the trustee and against the debtor. That is a matter which will eventually find its way to the judicial committee of the Privy Council. In fact all tliese questions-that is the rights of the parliament of Canada as against the provincial legislatures to legislate in matters of bankruptcy- will in due course come before the judicial committee of the Privy Council and will be dealt with there. If it is found they are unconstitutional it will be so declared and we will be where we were before; but it is not for us, sitting here as the parliament of Canada, to ask that the law be repealed while these questions are before the courts. The reason of much of this controversy is that in Quebec the law prior to this act differed so materially from the law of the other provinces that it is a bit of a shock to most of us in Quebec to find that our law in these particular matters should be overruled, as it were, by the federal authorities. But as I said before, the right was given to the parliament of Canada to do this, and until that right is taken away we are only exercising that right in a logical and constitutional way by enacting a law of this kind.
Many of my hon. friends were in this House in the parliament of 1917; they will remember that resolutions were passed by every board of trade in the country, with perhaps, one or two exceptions, by public bodies throughout the entire land, by the board of trade of the city of Montreal, the most important body of its kind in Canada, by boards of trade of Toronto and other cities, in fact, even by the board of trade of the city of Quebec, beseeching us to enact a law of this kind, and we were simply concurring in the views of the vast body of the people at the time when this law was passed. I care not for the odium which appears to have been cast upon me by certain people in Quebec for my part in putting upon the statute books this particular act. My friends will probably come to see a little later on that I was right when I advocated a law of this kind for the entire Dominion. The suggestion, as I said before, of contracting the province of Quebec out of this act will meet with my uncompromising opposition, and I would much rather see the act thrown into the waste paper basket holus-bolus than agree to any scheme which would put Quebec into one class and the rest of Canada into another. Such action does not make for nationhood, concord or harmony. It is true that we have on the statute books certain acts which permit Quebec in specific matters to pass its own laws. The one I have
in mind is the Lord's Day Act; but surely we cannot begin to make any comparison between the Lord's Day Act and the Bankruptcy Act. The Lord's Day Act is an act for the observance of Sunday, and of Saturday, if I may say so. The act of Quebec is the most fair-minded and broadest of its kind in the whole Dominion. It declares that any person who keeps Saturday as his day of rest may work on Sunday, and that the laws and customs of Quebec as regards the observance of Sunday shall remain in force notwithstanding the federal Lord's Day Act. I should be the last one to complain about the Lord's Day Act in Quebec, because I had something to do in seeing that the proviso as regards Saturday observance was inserted in that act. Tou cannot compare an act which deals with the trade and commerce of this country with the Lord's Day Act. Trade and commerce is the same in every part of Canada; the other act is a.matter of religious principle and observance, and we cannot think for a moment of placing the Bankruptcy Act in the same category as the Lord's Day Act. For these reasons, I shall vote against the resolution which was introduced by the hon. member for Charlevoix-Montmorency.
