speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I always listen with a great deal of interest to the hon. member for George Etienne Cartier (Mr. Jacobs) and again to-night, I was charmed to hear his eloquence as he spoke on -may I say?-so difficult a subject as the Bankuptcy Act. There is however, a point as regards which I cannot agree with my hon. friend, and there is at least one assertion which he has made that I must challenge. He seems to think that Le Devoir is the guiding influence of hon. members from Quebec. In that respect, my hon. friend is altogether wrong. We read Le Devoir at least, I do; I take what good there is in it and what I think is wrong, I leave out. In this particular case, it just happens that Le Devoir has been conducting a campaign against this law, and I think Le Devoir is perfectly right in doing so. That is the reason why to-day we stand with Le Devoir. I wish also to say to my hon. friend that in opposing this law, we rest our opinions on its merits only. We are not afraid by any means, nor are we prejudiced by the fact that the English law might be introduced into this country, and more particularly into Quebec. We want laws which are just and right to be introduced into this country; but we are opposed to laws that are unjust and vicious and, in our opinion, this law is both unjust and vicious. Rightly or wrongly, I am one of those who have always opposed this law. I have made strong
Bankruptcy

representations, and I have brought protests to members of this government and the preceding government. Some amendments have been brought up; but I do not think this law is subject to amendment in order to make it right and just, because the fundamental principle of the law is, in my opinion, wrong and bad. The hon. member for George Etienne Cartier thought, doubtless, that he had driven a very strong point when he said that this law was simply a replica of an old law that was passed in England about forty years ago. If there is a reason why I would not have this law in Canada, it is because it is a replica of an English law, passed some forty years ago. We have had too much copying of English laws in this country. We have this law which is a copy of the English law; we have another law7, which in my opinion, is bad in many respects, which is also to a large extent a copy of the English law, and that is the electoral law. In many respects the electoral law has given us sad experiences. That law, in my judgment, was drafted by pseudo-experts or reformists, whose lack of experience and ignorance of conditions that prevail in this country are exceeded only by their arrogant self-appreciation. These men have shackled and fettered the electorate of this country with a cumbersome and, in many respects, unjust law imported from England where conditions are totally different from those which prevail ip this country, and to bring a law of this kind into Canada, the best argument that they have given us so far, is that it is a copy of the English law. Conditions in this country are altogether different from conditions in Europe and it is not because this bankruptcy law and this electoral law are copies of English laws that I object to them; I object to them because they are not suited to the people of Canada. I would object to them just as strongly if they had been imported from France.
While I am on this subject, I might have a word to say to my friends of the party angularly opposite. I have just said that the electoral law is bad in many respects. I will ask them what they think of that law when they consider the results that have just taken place as regards the contestation of the constituency of Moose Jaw? Is it not a fact that the hon. gentleman who was recently disqualified had, during the conduct of the election, committed no crime? I am sure many hon. gentlemen thought what that hon. gentleman did was absolutely correct and lawful. But this law, borrowed from England, has been drafted in such a way that it requires highly trained legal minds to understand and apply

it. And, so long as the law stands as we have it members of parliament will, quite unconsciously, do things that are not lawful; they will be liable to find themselves disqualified for having committed acts which are unlawful, although they may not have had the least idea that what they were doing was wrong. The electoral law must be modified in many respects if this condition of things is to be remedied. I mention this only by way of comparison in reference to the argument brought forward by my hon. friend from George Etienne Cartier (Mr. Jacobs), who declares that the law we are at present discussing is good because it is an English law.

it is the cardinal function of any government to give good laws to its people. I submit that this law as presented to the pepple of Canada, and as it stands to-day, is not a good law. My hon. friend for South Wellington (Mr. Guthrie) rose this afternoon and spoke in defence of the law, and I can quite understand his doing so if he assumes a share of the l esponsibility for it. back to the act itself, I shall be very brief. I believe that it should be limited to traders and that people who are not traders should not be allowed to fail. Reasons have been given on this point, and I will not repeat them. Then the proceedings under the Bankruptcy Act should be held at the place of the domicile of the insolvent. It is absolutely ridiculous, as at present, to allow a man living in Ottawa to go and fail in Toronto, or a man living in Fort William to fail in Ottawa, And this condition of things exists in Quebec; these anomalies have been observed.
A third point: I would object to property which has been given as security being sold to pay the costs of an insolvent estate. In other words, where property has been given as security it should stand as such, and the liquidator or the trustee should not have the right to take the proceeds of secured property to pay the fees of liquidation. Further, I submit that there should be inspectors for each province. There is no question that several trustees have violated the law. Well, hon. members say, go after them; why do you not take action against them? Now, Mr. Speaker, it is not every day that a man is

willing to lose his money in an insolvent estate, and then spend more good money taking an action against trustees. In that way, in ninety-nine cases out of a hundred the trustee gets away with it. I would also have the number of trustees limited. However, this is a point on which vye are not . all at one.' As to the tariff, I think it is not clear enough. The costs are far too high, too, and the tariff should be so drafted as to avoid such cases as have been cited this afternoon.
There is another point which has not been laised, and it is this. Under the act any trustee can go before a judge and ask for an ex parte ruling.	I submit that that is not
right or proper. It is absolutely contrary to the laws of procedure and justice that a person interested in a bankruptcy case should go before a judge and obtain such a ruling because no matter how just and honest the judge may be he knows the facts from one side only when an ex parte case is submitted to him, and in many cases injustice has been done. Moreover, we have seen cases in which the judge having rendered an ex parte ruling, the party who was dissatisfied with it has appeared before another judge and obtained a second ex parte ruling, overruling the first one. Perhaps I might mention on this point something that was said to me not later than three or four weeks ago by a Montreal lawyer. I do not know whether my hon. friend from George Etienne Cartier knows him, but I will not divulge his name. What he told me is worth listening to. Indeed prior to that time we had a bankruptcy act but it proved so unsatisfactory in operation that it was eventually repealed. Now the present bankruptcy law does not satisfy a large section of the people of this country. Leaving all technicalities aside, why not let us try to give satisfaction to all the people? I submit that this end can be served by letting those

provinces which are satisfied with this law retain it, giving the same liberty of action to other provinces which are dissatisfied to reject this legislation.
This is a very serious question. As the hon. member for South Wellington (Mr. Guthrie) stated this afternoon, complaints against the unsatisfactory operation of the act have been received from all the provinces. The hon. member said that these complaints were not against the principle of the law but against the amendments. Therefore I say again that when these complaints are so general, that when the law is so doubtful in its constitutionality, and when in the opinion of the people of Quebec it is bad in principle, why should it be forced on any province?
I have said that in the province of Quebec nearly everybody is against this law. I have before me an article which was published in the Montreal Gazette on the 5th December last. I shall not take up the time of the House by quoting it at length, but, generally, it states that the legislature of the province of Quebec was seized of the question and that the premier and all his cabinet had declared themselves against the Bankruptcy Act.

But I would not take from my hon. friends any benefit which in their opinion this law confers on them, and, on that account, failing to have it repealed I would have its operation confined to those provinces that desire to retain the benefits which they feel they derive from its provisions. subsubtopic: PROPOSED ABROGATION OR AMENDMENT OF BANKRUPTCY ACT, 1919
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it will soon be a century since the legislatures of this country started trying to give to the people a satisfactory bankruptcy law, and from what I have heard during the course of this debate, which I have followed with great interest, I am led to believe that we will have to spend the balance of the century in efforts to arrive at the desideratum.
Prior to confederation the provinces of Nova Scotia, New Brunswick and Ontario had at different periods legislated in regard to insolvency. None of these provinces ever passed any bankruptcy act. The province of Prince Edward Island had various statutes about insolvency, and in 1868 it adopted a regular bankruptcy act providing for the discharge of the debtor. The colony of Vancouver Island and the mainland colony of British Columbia always referred to the English law on insolvency and bankruptcy matters until they came into this confederation. It was the old province of Quebec, then Lower Canada, which was the first colony to legislate on bankruptcy. In 1839 it passed an ordinance entitled "An Ordinance concerning Bankrupts and the Administration and Distribution of their Estates." It was administered by commissioners. It applied to traders only. It provided for the discharge of the debtor, and it was based on the English law.
In 1843, under the Union, another bankruptcy act was passed. It repealed the ordinance of 1839. It applied to traders only of the two Canadas, and provided for the discharge of the debtor. Twenty-one years later, in 1864 an insolvency act, which was a bankruptcy act was passed. It applied to the traders of Quebec and applied also to all persons in Ontario. It provided for the discharge of the debtor, and was administered by official trustees.
Under the confederation the first statute passed on that subject was adopted in 1869. That statute repealed the Insolvency Act of 1864. It was a consolidation, an assimilation, of all the insolvency and bankruptcy legislation of the four provinces of Nova Scotia, New Brunswick, Quebec and Ontario. It repealed all the acts or parts of acts inconsistent with the legislation of 1869. The 97
statute of 1869, as well as the statute of 1864, provided for the discharge of the debtor. In 1875 another bankruptcy act was passed. By that statute the legislation of 1864 and of 1869 were repealed; also the statute of Prince Edward Island of 1896 was repealed. So with the legislation of Vancouver Island of 1862, and with the British Columbia legislation of 1865 which were repealed with all the amendments.
From the very start of the operation of that legislation of 1875, there was an agitation in the whole of this country, an irritation which became so acute that the law had to be repealed in 1880. As you have heard many times to-day, in 1918 the hon. member for George Etienne Cartier (Mr. Jacobs) introduced into this House a bankruptcy bill, which was very carefully studied, and distributed to the public after it had been reported from the committee, and we may properly say that this bill of the hon. member for George Etienne Cartier was the genesis of the statute of 1919.
This, Mr. Speaker, is to show and to establish that we have had many experiences in insolvency legislation and bankruptcy matters. This experience of ours, our neighbours have had. They have been working for nearly a century to arrive at the legislation which they have now, and which seems to be accepted by the people of the United States. Their first legislation was passed in 1800. It was repealed in 1803. A second bankruptcy act was adopted in 1841 and repealed two years after, in 1843. Only twenty-three years later, in 1867, a third statute was adopted, which endured until 1878. The law now in force in the United States was adopted in 1898.
This, Mr. Speaker, I repeat, establishes that we have had the same difficulties in Canada that they have had in the United States on this very important question of bankruptcy. But, after listening to the very able speeches which we have heard to-day, at what conclusion can we arrive if not this, that the best we can do would be to amend the statute on bankruptcy which is now on our books? The people of Canada, I repeat, for nearly one hundred years, not only in the western provinces and the eastern provinces but in Quebec as well, have been trying to get a satisfactory bankruptcy law, and as I have told you, it was the province of Quebec which was the first province to legislate on that matter. The social and economic needs of this country, I would say, demand that we should have a uniform law on bankruptcy, and if I am a good judge of public opinion I believe that a

Bankruptcy

majority of the people of Canada, Quebec included, are in favour of a bankruptcy law provided it is a fair bankruptcy law. If we were to repeal the law that we have to-day, which has been in force since 1920, on account of the abuses which have been cited to this House, then immediately after this session, or within a year anyhow, an agitation would be started in all the provinces of this Dominion to have in Canada bankruptcy legislation, as all the civilized people of the world have it. This same irritation, this same dissatisfaction which we have witnessed, would certainly result in the passing of a new law. But the day must come when in this country we shall have only one law on bankruptcy matters.
The proposition was made to the effect that we might perhaps keep on our statute books the bankruptcy law that we have, but make an exception of the province of Quebec. Is that practical? Is that advisable? Would it be wise? Would it be advantageous to the people of the province of Quebec?

speechtext:
I would not like to give an answer on that. Perhaps it may be possible, and perhaps not. At any rate I wish to say that the province of Quebec has in its territory some of the best traders of Canada. We have many important manufactures. We deal not only in the province of Quebec, but we deal all over Canada, and even supposing that we would accept the proposition put before the House, that the province of Quebec should not be under the Bankruptcy law, that law would nevertheless affect the manufacturers, merchants and all the creditors in the province of Quebec in their dealings with merchants, manufacturers and others residing in the other provinces and who might take advantage of the bankruptcy law, and I do not see really, even if we consider only the interests of the population of Quebec, what advantage we could find in accepting such a proposition.
I have listened with great attention to all the arguments brought forward in the course of this debate. I have noticed all the objections offered against the law as we have it to-day, and I must say none of these arguments, none of these objections, appeals strongly enough to me to convince me that we should repeal that law.
Mention was made of the fact that in the province of Quebec there were bills of costs which were extraordinarily high. It is possible the same thing may have happened in some of the other provinces of the Dominions, but it seems to me this is not an ob-

jection sufficient to justify the repeal of such an important law. I think it would be easy to find a remedy for such a condition. As to the right or the privilege which has been granted to the farmers in this country to take advantage of the law, even supposing the majority of this House would be disposed to accept this proposition, and to say the farmers should not be allowed to assign, this is not an objection against the principle of the law itself. Speaking for myself, Mr. Speaker, I must say that the moment that we adopt in this country a law of bankruptcy-that is to say, the right of the debtor to assign and the right of the creditor to force the debtor to assign, a law which provides for the administration and the liquidation of the estate of the debtor and provides for the discharge of the debtor under certain conditions-I cannot see very well how we could say, "because you are a merchant, because you are a manufacturer, you will have the advantage of that law, but the farmer will not; the farmer will not have the right to obtain his discharge if he is unhappy, if he has bad debts or is passing through bad times." On that point we are disposed to treat all our citizens alike. It seems to me we should not give any preference or any privilege to any class of our countrymen. We are told that some of the trustees have acted in a fraudulent manner, and that for that reason we should repeal the law of 1920. You have already been told, Mr. Speaker, that it would be very easy to find a method by which a trustee could be punished and placed in a position where it would be impossible for him to repeat the fraud. I have heard with pleasure hon. members who addressed the House and complimented the province of Quebec on the legislation we had regarding assignments. They were right. By experience I know that our law of Quebec gave full satisfaction to our people, and it was approved by all the citizens of Canada who knew of it. Perhaps, Mr. Speaker, we could succeed in amending our law of 1920 in such a manner that we would give to it the good character which we find in our Quebec law, and the good provisions which made it so acceptable to our population. I feel confident that the hon. members who spoke against the law of 1920 would be disposed to accept it. For my part the great source of all these troubles in the administration of our bankruptcy law is to be found in the manner in which the trustees are appointed. There are two modes of the administration of the estates of bankrupts. One is by trustees who are officially appointed by the state, responsible to the state and the state responsible for them, and the other

Bankruptcy
mode is trustees unofficially appointed by the creditors, for the benefit and the advantage of the creditors. Under the law of Quebec as we had it, we had no official trustees. There was no restriction as to the number of those who wished to become trustees. Any citizen in Quebec had the right to act as a trustee. The trustee was chosen and elected by the creditors. If we could arrive at the same system which prevailed in Quebec for so many years, and which proved absolutely acceptable to the people of Quebec and to all the creditors all over Canada, I think we would have found a solution of the troubles we meet to-day. Mr. Speaker, that is the system that they have :n England. I read from Duncan. Lav and Practice of Bankruptcy in Ci.n ida.
The system under the English act is a compromise between official and unofficial administration. The act provides for official receivers who act under the board of trade. Pending the appointment of a trustee the official receiver is interim receiver of the debtor's estate. He summons and presides at the first meeting of creditors; reports to the creditors any proposal which the debtor may have made with respect to the mode of liquidating his affairs; investigates the conduct of the debtor and takes part in the public examination of the debtor. After thus as it were, getting the bankruptcy proceedings under way the official receiver hands over to a trustee appointed by the creditors.
That is what we have been doing in Quebec for over twenty years, and if we were to adopt that in our act I think, Mr. Speaker, that it would give satisfaction to all the provinces of Canada. It has been suggested that instead of centralizing the administration of the Bankruptcy Act we should decentralize it. If we were to adopt the system they have in England, and that we had in the province of Quebec, we would be carrying out decentralization. The debtors would assign to the prothonotary or at the court house, and this would harmonize with the proposition which is put before the House.
I do not know what the hon. member for Charlevoix-Montmorency (Mr. Casgrain) will say in reply. I hope, however, that he will not insist on pressing this proposition to a vote. Even after listening to his very able address, and to all the other speeches which were delivered to-day, it seems to me that very few members would be perpared to take the responsibility of asking for the repeal of the bankruptcy law that we now have. Most of us-I will say every one of us-in this House are agreed as to the necessity of the law being amended. If the hon. member struck out the last part of his resolution and simply asked that the law be amended I am sure the resolution would then pass unanimously. For my part I would be happy to
97 i
vote in favour of such a resolution as amended. At any rate, after the remarks which have been made during this very interesting debate I may say that the government is disposed to submit to the consideration of the House during the present session some amendments to the act. We will try and make them as complete as possible so that all the provinces of the Dominion will be able to say, after those amendments have been made, that the law on bankruptcy matters is acceptable to them.

speechtext:
We have all, no doubt, listened with much interest to the speech of the Minister of Justice, and particularly to his resume of the evolution of the Bankruptcy Act. I must say, however, that I do not feel that I can accept the suggestion which he made to the mover of the resolution, or rather I do not feel that if that hon. gentleman accepted the suggestion of the Minister of Justice I would be prepared to vote for the resolution in its amended form. My reason for taking that stand is, that if the words "or abrogated" were eliminated from the resolution its wording would still be very indefinite. It would then read that the Bankruptcy Act should be amended. That does not mean anything at all. It might mean amended by striking out one word, or it might mean amended by striking out the whole of the act except one word. It seems to me that we should have something more definite from the minister, that we should have some concrete proposition before us for our consideration before we could vote intelligently on any resolution of this kind.
I think the mover of the resolution was quite justified in bringing the matter to the attention of the House. I realize the fact that conditions as to the administration of this act in the province of Quebec cannot be very satisfactory. As to that, of course, I do not know the details other than what have been given here to-day. That same conditions do not obtain in all the other provinces so far as my information goes or, I should say, at least, not in the province of British Columbia so far as I am aware. We have found there that the act is being administered in a fairly satisfactory manner. To the best of my information those who were appointed to act as trustees in British Columbia were men or companies who were responsible parties, and who attempted to carry out the provisions of the act in a fair and reasonable manner. It may be that in the province of Quebec too many trustees have been appointed.
Bankruptcy

I listened, too, with a good deal of astonishment to the remarks of the hon. member for Chambly and Vercheres (Mr. Archambault). (Sometimes the hon. gentleman tries to be serious but usually he is quite the reverse, and I was at a loss this afternoon to know whether to take him seriously or otherwise. He made the statement that the appointment of trustees in the province of Quebec had been made through the exercise of political patronage. I asked the hon. gentleman if he knew of one case where an application for appointment as trustee, properly supported by the necessary bond, had been refused and he said, "no", and that he had not made an investigation into that feature at all. But he had a lot of cases that he referred to in other connections, and it seems to me that if there had been such a case the hon. gentleman would have known about it. My information is that appointments were made in all cases where the trustee, or the proposed trustee, .would provide a bond for $10,000 to properly administer his duties. I had occasion, I remember, at one time to make inquiries as to what the requirements were to obtain an appointment under the act, and I was told that there was no restriction whatever, absolutely none, but that anyone who applied and put up this bond could be appointed. Well, that principle may be objectionable, and apparently it has worked out in the province of Quebec in such a way, according to hon. members who have spoken, that too many trustees have been appointed. But it is not a case of political patronage at all, there is no political patronage about it, and I was very much surprised to hear the hon. member make the accusation on such a flimsy foundation.
I listened with some interest to the remarks of the hon. member for Joliette (Mr. Denis). I always listen to the hon. gentleman with interest. I feel that invariably he is sincere and in most cases I have found him to be reasonable. The hon. member is always fair in his arguments, is usually rather
10 p.m. convincing, and generally has grounds for every proposition that he submits. I was therefore surprised to-day to hear the argument that he advanced against this act. He stated that the act should be repealed because it was draughted along the lines of an English act. He seems to wish to have the House think it was a good and sufficient reason for asking for the repeal of any act, that it was made in England, as it were, or that it was modelled after an English act. That is a very surprising proposition to me. I thought in this country 
we got most of our good models of law from England; that they were always safe guides for us to use. Indeed, I think both my hon. friend and myself found in our practise of law that the English law is pretty good; that English cases are pretty sound; that English precedents are very reliable, and that when we follow them, we are usually on safe ground. The hon. member departed somewhat from his customary course, and he got lost in the fog, or something of that kind, when he touched upon that subject. I see that he is smiling now; I am sure that he has come to his senses again, and that if he had opportunity to do so, he would withdraw that as a ground of opposition to this particular law.

Perhaps my hon. friend would like to hear some more recommendations of himself, but I am afraid I have complimented him enough for one evening. I entirely agree with those hon. gentlemen who have stated their adherence to the policy of uniformity of laws in this Dominion of ours. We must all appreciate the movement which is now on foot, in which you, Mr. Speaker, are playing some part, which is tending to-

Bankruptcy
wards bringing together the people of Canada for the welfare of this great Dominion. It would be a mistake, particularly as regards such an important matter as this, to have one law in Quebec and another law for the other provinces. Some hon. gentlemen, and particularly the hon. member for Joliette (Mr. Denis), put this query to the House: Why should we in Quebec be forced to take something that we do not want? Of course, that would be a hard question to answer if his facta were correct. After listening to the remarks of the Minister of Justice (Sir Lomer Gouin), I am forced to the conclusion that it would be going a little far to say that the people of Quebec, as a whole, are asking for the repeal of this particular enactment. I do not think that can be shown, because, if I remember correctly, the act was originally introduced by a Quebec member, and when it came up during the last parliament and prior to its being passed, there was plenty of time for objection to be made to it. If I remember correctly, the province of Quebec was not as a whole opposed to it in fact, I do not remember that there was any very strenuous opposition from Quebec. But in Quebec, as in other places, there were strong and urgent demands for the passage of such a law. That is as far as my memory goes. I know there were strong demands from other parts of Canada, and those demands were based on the fact that there was so much diversity in the matter of assignments and the winding-up of estates by reason of insolvency, that business concerns which did business in a big way, were unable to tell, with any degree of certainty, exactly what the real conditions were.
I am not going to go over the ground at any length; but I think I am safe in saying that there was on the part of the business people of Canada a very strong demand that there be a uniform bankruptcy law, and this law was passed as a result of that demand. Whj7 should we repeal the law altogether? Why cannot we rather have put up to us in concrete form some amendment or amendments which will meet the difficulties which have been encountered, so that .they may be considered, and then I am sure it will be possible, as the Minister of Justice says, to work out an act that will be satisfactory to the province of Quebec? Why should the act be repealed? Personally, I am opposed to its being repealed, and I am also opposed to voting for a resolution which calls for the amendment or the repeal of an act. We should either have certain amendments or the repeal of the act proposed; then either proposition would be open for anyone to vote on, and I
would certainly vote against the repeal of the act.
Something has been said about the costs being excessive, and it may be that in some cases the costs have been excessive. But, as I say, that is also a matter that can be remedied. If the costs are too high surely we can put into the act a schedule of costs that would be satisfactory to those who are complaining. But it seems to me that the real objection to the act, so far as the province of Quebec is concerned, is that too many trustees have been appointed, and that these trustees have been endeavouring to get business for themselves, and consequently have created difficulties which have given rise to this agitation. Well, that also is a matter that can be remedied. It would be possible, surely, to revise the list of trustees appointed for the province of Quebec, and more particularly for Montreal, if there are too many there, and reduce the number. To my mind that would meet the situation. I believe that after the courts have had time to interpret the act, after the law has become settled, and after the necessary amendments have been made, we shall find that the act will work smoothly enough and that it will be more satisfactory to have one uniform bankruptcy law for the whole of Canada than that there should exist such a condition as we had prior to the passing of the act.

speechtext:
I wish to speak briefly on the resolution, and in doing so I shall 'approach the subject from my limited experience of the working of the act in the province of Ontario. I hope, however, that in dealing with it I shall not consider it from a provincial standpoint, but that whatever I may say will have reference to the matter upon the national scale and with a view to the benefit of Canada at large. Now, the resolution makes two attacks on this piece of legislation, and it appears to me that these attacks are somewhat inconsistent. First, it suggests the repeal of the act; and then, as if the mover were not confident as to the advisability of that, it proposes an amendment to it. There is considerable inconsistency in the proposition outlined in the resolution itself. We cannot overemphasize the importance of uniformity in our bankruptcy law in Canada. Our commerce has become very widely extended, and in my own limited experience I have found great difficulty in advising a creditor with respect to his rights when he was carrying on business in all the nine provinces of the Dominion under the old system. In the case
Bankruptcy

of insolvency in one province, his rights would be governed by the laws of that province, and in another province his rights might be altogether different. The result was that we had nine different rights in the Dominion of Canada, all in connection with one situation, that of insolvency. We have been endeavouring through our Dominion Law Association to bring about uniformity in the laws relating to matters of this kind, and this surely is one in regard to which it is very important that there should be that uniformity which this statute provides. I cannot understand any reason why all classes of the community should not be free to take advantage of the act; I cannot see why the farmer should not be as free to assign and get a discharge as is a trader and do not think that anything has been said in support of that contention that requires any answer. I submit that after listening to the clear, complete and concise review of the situation by the Minister of Justice (Sir Lomer Gouin) the answer to the resolution has. been provided, and nothing can be added to what he has said. This legislation was not hurriedly introduced; it was preceded by a long campaign of education, and after representations had been made from different parts of the country in favour of a Dominion insolvency law. The act has many advantages. It has the advantage of uniformity, and a creditor knows his rights to be the same in all provinces. It has made a good beginning and has worked well in the province of Ontario. No person contends that it is perfect; it does need some amendment, and the weakness of it is particularly striking in its tendency to centralization. That was pointed out by one of the preceding speakers and a remedy was suggested.. If there are any features in the law of the province of Quebec, as it existed prior to this act, that are better than the law we now have, or that are an improvement upon it, then by all means let us have them and embody them in the act. There will be no objection to them on the ground that they come from the province of Quebec, for we wish to make the law as perfect as we can. I am sure that it makes for a common citizenship to have a law of this kind. I am strongly opposed to the repeal of the act, but am in favour of its amendment in every respect that will make it more workable, that will improve it, and that will meet the defects which experience from time to time show's that it possesses. For that reason I am opposed to the resolution in so far as it asks for the repeal of the act, while I am in favour of the suggestion of the Minister of Justice that it be amended.

speechtext: Before the debate is concluded I might offer a few remarks. I should riot like the resolution to be voted upon without putting before the House this fact, that the resolution is not submitted because the province of Quebec, from which I come, is afraid of any invasion of English law under the new system. But the debate that has occurred to-day must have shown conclusively to every hon. gentleman that there are undoubtedly real defects in the law; and as was pointed out by the hon. member for George Etienne Cartier, the act is nothing but a replica of the English law. We are not afraid of having certain provisions of the laws of other countries embodied in our law, provided that under all circumstances the rights of each and every province of this Dominion be properly safeguarded and protected. And that is why in the remarks I made this afternoon before closing my address I requested the hon. the Minister of Justice to see to it that in all cases the laws of the province of Quebec should be respected, and the rights of the people adequately protected. In view of the clear address of the minister and the sound views he expressed [DOT] regarding the question of the abrogation of the law, and his opinion as to what should be done under the circumstances, I have no objection to accepting his suggestion. I would therefore move to strike out the last two words of the resolution. So that the motion will not now be to the effect that in the opinion of this House the law as it stands at present should be amended provided, as the Minister of Justice pointed out in the course of his remarks, that it be in such terms as shall be in the best interests of the whole, community.

speakeroldname: Mr. C. G. POWER (Quebec South) moved:
speechtext:
That, in the opinion of this House, it is expedient to declare that save in the case of actual invasion the Dominion of Canada shall not be committed to participation in any war without the consent of the parliament of Canada.
He said: Mr. Speaker, lest later on in the course of the debate some hon. gentleman may accuse me of political embezzlement and literary plagiarism, I wish at the outset to plead guilty to both charges. The resolution which I have placed on the order paper is taken mutatis mutandis from Article 48 of the constitution of the Irish Free State. This constitution was ratified by the parliament of Great Britain.
The theories advanced and the arguments adduced in support thereof have been placed before the people of this country on numerous occasions by Mr. John S. Ewart, K.C., of Ottawa. Mr. Ewart, in a manner as able as unselfish, has for a number of years devoted himself to the study of Canada's relations to the Empire and to the rest of the world. He has done this without any hope of financial reward or political preferment. His theory has developed into this: That we in Canada at this stage of our national development should be the moulders of our own destiny, undeterred by any consideration of interest or sentiment, except the interest which we have in matters pertaining to our own country and the natural affection which every Canadian should have for the land of his birth or of his adoption.
Some hon. gentlemen may be of opinion that this resolution is somewhat inopportune. Others may be of opinion that it is unnecessary because by the very fact that no moneys can be appropriated without the vote of this parliament, therefore no Canadian troops can be equipped or put in a state to go to war. It is urged that no government unless it had the support of the House of Commons or was assured of such support, could possibly involve Canada in war.
To the first of these objections, I answer that now is the time, if ever, for us to approve or disapprove of the. conduct of the
present administration during the Near Eastern crisis of last September, that now is the time, not too soon after the actual event for us to be still under the spell of the enthusiasm and of the glamour of the moment and not too far removed for us not to understand perfectly and to judge impartially as to what occurred on that occasion.
My answer to those who might say that this resolution is unnecessary is that as a matter of fact on the last two occasions on which Canadian troops have taken part in war they were mobilized and prepared for embarkation before even our parliament was summoned.
I would say further that the resolution does not pretend so much to discuss the actual participation of this country in war as its commitment to participation. I think that perhaps as I proceed with my argument I can place this point more clearly before the House.
There are in this country two great schools of thought: Those who say-as some hon. gentlemen said last September-that at the moment when Great Britain extended to us an invitation to mobilize our troops for the Gallipoli campaign, we should instantly have answered, "Ready! aye ready!" Others who say "It was well that we had a government in power courageous enough to answer to the invitation of the British Prime Minister: 'Let us see what this quarrel is about-what are our interests *-how is Canada's honour involved-is her territorial integrity menaced?' "
Now, Sir, I should like for a few moments to discuss the point of view of those who are willing to ask the Dominion to take part in any and every war wherein the British Empire may be engaged. From what I can gather their arguments-and they are not many-may be classified somewhat as follows: First, what I may call the sentimental argument; next, the moral argument; and last the legal or constitutional argument.
The sentimental argument may be summed up somewhat in these words: We must help the Mother Country-blood is thicker than water-we must answer the call of the blood. To this I would reply: In the first place, Britain is not our Mother Country; France is. It was the French explorers, the French missionaries,- the French captains who first laid the foundations of civilization in this country, who first developed and christianized it. It was the French explorers who first opened up this country to civilization, and if we have a mother country at all in that sense, it must surely be France. Now I hardly think that any member of this House will venture to assert that we should go to war on any occasion when France is at war.
Canada and War

There is another argument, too, under the same heading, the argument of the call of the blood. Because the greater proportion of the inhabitants of Canada are of British birth or descent it is urged that we should promptly enter into bellicose and belligerent operations as soon as the Mother Country of these individuals becomes involved in war. We might just as well say that the United States should become involved in war when Britain is at war, because I imagine that the greater number of inhabitants of the United States have ties of kindred or business more or less closely connected with people living in the Old Country. But even admitting that this argument is not a good one, I would ask hon. members whether they think it is fundamentally and morally sound for the majority of the inhabitants of this country, simply because they are bound by ties of blood and sympathy to some nation, to insist that their fellow-citizens of some other nationality or of different racial descent should kill or be killed for the sake of whatever sympathy the first nationality may have. In this country there are people of every race and of every nationality. When they become citizens of Canada they are entitled to equal rights, and particularly to that right and privilege of carrying on their affairs in a manner to become as prosperous as possible, and unless we give them security to pursue their peaceful avocations free from the troubles and turmoil of war we have not carried out our contract with them.
Then we have what is called the moral argument, which might be summed up as follows. As Canadians we owe to the British Empire or to Great Britain that we have been protected by the British army and the British navy, and furthermore we owe to Great Britain our constitutional development and the freedom and privileges we enjoy under the British Constitution.
To that first argument I answer this: We have not, as a, matter of fact, been protected to any great extent by the British army. On two occasions on which we became involved in war, when the British army fought on our side, the war was none of our choosing. The war of American Independence was certainly not brought on by Canada or by the citizens of Canada. With the war of 1812 we had little or nothing to do, and the least that those who undertook to carry on this war could do was to protect their own base. Canada on both these occasions was the base of supplies for the British army in their attacks against the United States and in their defence against attacks from that country. Further-

more, if British troops have for a long time garrisoned this country, I submit that it was
because it suited the convenience of the Imperial authorities and not because it suited our convenience. In that connection may I quote the opinion expressed by the Duke of Newcastle before a select committee of the British House of Commons in 1881. He was asked the following question:
Since 1854, the time when the arrangement of which you spoke was made, it appears that the force in the North American Colonies has not been in a state of progressive reduction, but rather fluctuating.
His reply was:
I have already stated in answer to some questions in the early part of my examination that that was done without any communication with the colony, and for Imperial purposes. It was a convenience to us to send those troops there; they were not required by the Colony and beyond the towns and villages in which they were placed, which no doubt derived advantages from the commissariat, I do not think that the colony wished a single man.
Further on in the same inquiry, Earl Grey states that the troops were in Canada, but they were here because they cost very little more than they would at home. I have a number of other quotations on the same subject, but as the hour is growing very late I shall not weary the patience of the House by giving them.
With regard to naval protection, it has been said frequently in this House and outside of it, where would Canada be if it had not, been for the protection of the British navy? The same argument applies also to the navy with regard to the war of 1812 and the war of American Independence. With regard to further protection, may I quote further from the evidence given before that same select committee of the British House of Commons'.' Rear Admiral Erskine states:
We are at a certain expense in defending Canada; but supposing Canada were incorporated into the United States, would our expense be increased or diminished in time of war?
His reply to this was:
Your expense must increase, because you must have your territory protected in the event of the Americans committing any aggression upon your trade, which now there is no apprehension of.
The Duke of Newcastle in the same inquiry states:
Halifax is not kept up for the benefit of Nova Scotia; but rightly or wrongly according to the particular views which men may entertain, it is kept for military purposes; it is still more important as a naval station, inasmuch as by its natural capabilities it is certainly one of the finest, and in all probability the finest harbour in the world.
I go further, apd I say that not only has the British navy not protected us, but it has on several occasions intervened to our disad-

Canada and War
vantage. I quote now from Canada and British Wars by John S. Ewart, K.C., Ottawa, who, at page 10, says:
Observe, next, that, so far from having enjoyed British protection, there have been but two occasions upon which the British navy has gone into action in connection with our (I include Newfoundland) quarrels, and in each case, although we were indubitably in the right, the British fleet acted against us. The first occasion was in connection with the seizure, by the United States cruisers, of our sealing ships on the open ocean. . . . The second occasion was when, in defence of an absurd claim of the French, a squad of British marines destroyed the lobster factories of Newfoundlanders on Newfoundland territory. In both of these' cases, not only was it the opinion of the British government that our opponents were undoubtedly wrong, but, in the international arbitration in the one case, and in the British Privy Council in the other, our contention was authoritatively declared to be right.
So we may conclude from these quotations and from our own experience that so far from our being protected by the British army or the British navy, we have in a large measure protected ourselves, and in some instances if we could we would have protected ourselves more strenuously against them.
It is urged also that our constitutional development, the constitutional freedom and rights and privilege that we now enjoy are due in a large measure to what I may call the benevolence of Breat Britain. Let us see what these blessings are.
The first important document in our constitutional history was the Constitution of 1791. That was granted to us shortly after the American Revolution. The reason given for advancing us so far along the path of freedom is somewhat as follows. Lord Grenville in a letter to Lord Dorchester about 1790 asks for his opinion on this question.
-by what means, the connection and dependence of Canada, on this country may be so preserved and cultivated, as to be rendered most beneficial to Great Britain during its continuance, and most permanent in its duration.
The Colonial Office accompanied these suggestions with the hope,-
-that they would afford a juster, and more effectual security against the growth of a republican or independent spirit, than any which could be derived from a government more arbitrary in its form or principles.
So that our constitution in 1791 was granted to us, not so much for our benefit as in order to keep us the longer under the more direct control and subjection of the Imperial authority. The next important step in our constitutional development was taken in 1841. I do not think it is necessary for me to dwell at any greater length on that portion of our history. We obtained a constitution in 1841 as a result of the rebellion in 1837. If we
were granted certain freedom it was because it was found impossible to govern Canada, a country so far removed from Great Britain, unless certain concessions were made, and before the concesions were made the colonies had broken out into open revolt. The next step in our constitutional history was the proclamation of 1867. I do not think there is any question of doubt whatsoever in the mind of any hon. member but that the motive which swayed the British government in granting us the British North America Act was in order that we would build up, under the auspices of the British gevemment, on the North American continent a country strong enough and big enough and having sufficient strength to resist any encroachment which the republic to the south of us might be able or willing to make on the British naval or military power. May I say further still on this subject that it is true that we obtained freedom and our present free institutions while under the protection of Great Britain, but I submit, Sir, there is no copyright on freedom. We could just as well have obtained that freedom and developed our own free institutions under the protection of any other power, or we could have obtained it even had we been free and independent. We owe every gratitude to the Mother of Parliaments for having so far developed parliamentary institutions, but there was no copyright, as I said before, and no law which prevented us from copying these institutions and applying them to our own circumstances.
To conclude this portion of my remarks, let me make a passing reference to our experience with British diplomacy when we were represented in foreign affairs by the British authorities. Every one in this House is familiar with the fact that after the war of the American revolution we lost a large portion of the territory that rightfully belonged to us and which now makes up a portion of the United States of America. Every one knows of the Hay-Ashburton Treaty by which we lost Maine. Every one knows of our fishery dispute, and every one knows of Sir John Macdonald's report when he was acting with certain British diplomats at Washington. He found they were not so much interested in Canada as they were anxious to get home with a treaty of some kind in their pockets. During the whole course of our empire when we were in early youth and in young manhood, we were protected, firstly-if we were protected at all-in order to suit the interests of the Mother Country, and as soon as it no longer suited their interests we were made the butt of their diplomacy in order to placate
Canada and War

and to please the Americans on every possible occasion. In making these remarks I wish not to be misinterpreted. I do not think there is any one on this side of the House, or on the other side of the House who shares this view with me wishes, for one instant, to decry the British Empire or its achievements. We are proud that we have taken part in some of these achievements. We are willing to admit that probably no empire in the world or no country in the world has done so much for the advancement of the human, race, but at the same time we would like it to be clearly understood just what our obligations and what our views on this question are.
Before closing this part of my argument allow me to discuss what might be called the legal and constitutional viewpoint. It is I think fairly well understood that during the whole course of British constitutional history, so far from the colonies being obliged to defend or to help the Mother Country, it was the duty of the dominant partner to extend aid and assistance to the colonies. We have but to contrast the state of affairs which existed on the North American continent during the wars which took place here between England and France to see what the distinction was between the two colonial policies. The French in Canada marched to war at the command of the King. The British in America marched to war, sent their troops to the frontiers, and granted supplies only when the American colonial assemblies voted such supplies. And so a contrast can be made through the whole course of British and colonial history. So much did the colonies have control of their own funds, and of the question of defence, that when it was attempted to tax them, they for purposes purely of their own defence rebelled, and during the course of that rebellion the British House of Commons decreed-
The King and parliament of Great Britain would not impose any duty, tax, or assessment whatever, payable in any of His Majesty's colonies, provinces and plantations in North America or the West Indies, except only such duties as it might be expedient to impose for the regulation of commerce; the net produce of such duties to be always paid and applied to and for the use of the colony, province or plantation in which the same shall be respectively levied, in such manner as other duties collected by the authority of the respective general courts or general assemblies of such colonies, provinces or plantations were ordinarily paid and applied.
Furthermore it has been stated by the foremost British authorities that the relation of the colonies to the Mother Country was not such that the Mother Country could not call
on the colony for aid and assistance. On the
contrary the Duke of Newcastle, in the same

inquiry which I have already mentioned, states in answer to questions;
Q. May your opinion be stated in these terms, that the mother country having assumed the government of a colony, takes upon itself all the responsibility of its defence?-A. Certainly.
Q. No responsibility given to a Colony gives it the responsibility of declaring war?-A. Certainly not.
Q. The power, therefore, of declaring war imposes upon the government the responsibility of protecting the Colony from the cost of war?-A. Certainly.
So that even during the time of our colonial status there was no question of doubt in the minds of British statesmen but that we were not under any obligation whatsoever to furnish it assistance.
Now, let us see what happened later on when we developed still more; when we lost the status of a colony and became a self-governing dominion and later on a nation. It was found and it was stated distinctly by our leaders, that the question of the defence of the Empire bad now become a matter of treaty obligation and no longer a matter of any kind of obligation. Sir John Macdonald, at the time of the Soudan war, stated in a letter to Sir Charles Tupper, the High Commissioner in London, dated 12th March, 1885, in refusing to furnish a contingent for that war:
Our men and money would therefore be sacrificed to get Gladstone and Co. out of the hole they have plunged themselves into by their own imbecility. Again the reciprocal aid to be given by the colonies and England should be a matter of treaty, deliberately entered into and settled on a permanent basis.
And then he goes on to say further:
The spasmodic offers of our Militia Colonels anxious for excitement or notoriety, have roused unreasonable expectations in England and are so far unfortunate. I dare say that a battalion or two of venturous spirits might be enlisted but 7 d.* a day will cool most men's warlike ardour.
Again, Sir Wilfrid Laurier, at the time of the despatch of the South African contingent
said:
I claim for Canada this, that in the future Canada shall be at liberty to act or not to act, to interfere or not to interfere, to do just as she pleases, and that she shall reserve to herself the right to judge whether or not there is cause for her to act.
This, Sir, 1 think is the present state of the case. We are not bound to take part in Britain's wars unless we have some kind of a treaty which would bind us to do so. This was the position last September. We had no treaty at that time. We were under no written obligation or, as I have shown, moral or legal obligation to send an expedition to the Far East, so that the government of this country, in acting as they did, I think acted constitutionally, acted within their rights, acted with perfect justice, and for that reason

Canada and War
deserves the thanks of the House and of the country.
That crisis having been safely passed let us see what shall be our policy for the future. I have said that in my opinion-and if the argument which I have pursued so far is right such is the case, any question of participation in Imperial wars should be a matter of treaty of arrangement. This resolution reads that no such treaty or arrangement be entered into without the consent of the parliament of Canada. In case it should be said that it would be impossible to enter into any such treaty or arrangement without the consent of parliament, allow me to give you an example of a case in which a country became involved in war without the consent of the people, or even the.consent of parliament. In making these remarks I do not wish to ascribe any blame of those concerned in Great Britai#. To my mind Great Britain entered the last war from the purest of motives, and after she had made every effort to avoid that calamity. She was, it is true, bound by no treaty obligation, but she was obliged to support France owing to a series of arrangements, conversations, and diplomatic interventions which allowed France to hope that in any case in which she should be assailed Britain would promptly come to her assistance. The obligation was, I say so strong that the parliament of great Britain- though it had no knowledge of these conversations or these arrangements-could not without besmirching the national honour, refuse to take part in the war. In 1904 Great Britain and France came to a sort of friendly arrangement whereby these two nations settled their difficulties throughout the world. One of the conditions was that France agreed to give Britain a free hand in Egypt and Britain agreed to give France a free hand in Morocco. In 1905 arose the first Moroccan incident. May I quote here the words of Sir Edward Grey from the Parliamentary Debates, British House of Commons, Volume 65, page 1,181:
Now I must make this question of obligation clear to the House. I must go back to the first Moroccan crisis of 1906. . . . when a general election was in progress, and ministers were scattered over the country; and-spending three days a week in my constituency and three days at the Foreign Office-was asked the question whether if that crisis developed into war between France and Germany we would give armed support. I said then that I could promise nothing to any foreign power unless it was subsequently to receive the whole-hearted support of public opinion here if the occasion arose. I said, in my opinion, if war was forced upon France then on the question of Morocco-a question which had just been the subject of agreement between this country and France, an agreement exceedingly popular on both sides-that if out of that agreement war was forced
on Fiance at that time, in my view public opinion in this country would have rallied to the material support of France.
He says, further on, that the French officials approached him saying: "It is all very well to state that you will support us in the case of war with Germany, but had we not better have some arrangement, some conversations, between the military advisers of both countries in order, if you find yourself bound to take part in this war, that we will be in a position to make reciprocal arrangements?" He says that he agreed to this arrangement. Then he goes on to say:
As I have told the House, upon that occasion a General Election was in prospect. I had to take the responsibility of doing that without the cabinet. It could not be summoned. An answer had to be given.
I	consulted Sir Henry Campbell-Bannerman, the Prime Minister; I consulted, I remember, Lord Haldane, who was then Secretary of State for war, and the present Prime Minister who was then Chancellor of the Exchequer. That was the most I could do, and they authorized that on the distinct understanding that it left the hands of the government free whenever the crisis arose.
Then he states that another Moroccan crisis arose, that of Agadir-
When was this speech delivered by Sir Edward Grey?

On the 3rd of August, 1914. Then, at the time of the Agadir crisis in 1912, he gave a somewhat similar assurance to the French Ambassador. It can clearly be shown by the diplomatic documents relating to the war that at that time, in 1912, conversations and reciprocal arrangements were
II	p.m. entered into between not only the
French general staff and the British general staff, but also the Belgium general staff and the British general staff. It is true that at that time the French Ambassador, at the request of Sir Edward Grey, gave him a letter in which this was stated:
We have agreed that consultation between experts is not and ought not to be regarded as an engagement that commits either government to action in a contingency that has not yet arisen and may never arise.
Other English statesmen, however, took a different view of those engagements from that which Sir Edward Grey took. It will be remembered that, at that time, owing to negotiations which had passed between the British and the French governments, the British fleet retired to the North sea and the French fleet retired to the Mediterranean, leaving the British fleet to undertake the defence of the North sea. Lord Crewe, on August 6, 1914, says:
The direct effect of that understanding was the weakening of the French maritime defence in the channel and the corresponding weakening of our

maritime defence in the Mediterranean. Your Lordships will see that the result was inevitable, without any formal arrangement between the two powers that one should fill the gap left by the other.
The Marquis of Lansdowne, speaking on the same day, August 6, 1914, states:
I do not think anyone can have failed to be deeply shocked by what I can now describe as the cynical attempt made to bribe this country, and not this country alone, into a disregard both of its treaty obligations and of those other obligations which are not less sacred because they are not embodied in a signed and sealed document. . . . To the other category belong our obligations to France -obligations of honour, which have grown up in consequence of the close intimacy by which the two nations have been united during the last few fateful years.
Bonar Law is of the same opinion in a letter which he wrote to Mr. Asquith, Prime Minister of England, on August 3, 1914. Lloyd George, in defending his policy in August, 1918, four years afterwards, stated that there could be no question of doubt but that an obligation of honour was imposed upon the British Empire to intervene in any war in which Germany should be the aggressor. I have said before that it is possible for obligations of this nature to be entered into without consultation with parliament and without the knowledge and consent of parliament. I have had in my hand a book entitled, How the Wat Came, by Earl Lorebum, who was from 1905 to 1912 Lord Chancellor, and consequently a member of the British cabinet. I may say that Sir Edward Grey, in the course of his speech, after stating that he had informed Sir Henry Campbell-Bannerman and others, states:
The fact that conversations between military and naval experts took place was later on-I think much later on because that crisis passed and the thing ceased to be of importance-leu later on it was brought to the knowledge of the cabinet.
This is what Lord Lorebum says:
He does not say when. . . . but one of Sir Edward Grey's then colleagues may be permitted, in view of his statement about withholding the information from the cabinet, to offer certain criticisms. Sir Edward Grey's phraseology rather conveys that his selection of confidants was casual, but Mr. Asquith and Lord Haldane were with himself vice-presidents of the Liberal leaguq,, a continuation of the Liberal imperialistic movement which had supported the South African war and opposed Sir Henry Campbell-Bannerman on that subject.
He says further:
There was no difficulty whatever in summoning the cabinet during the election to consider so grave a matter. A good many members of the cabinet were in London or within an hour of it, while those whom he consulted were at a distance. And there are "railways and post offices in Great Britain. The cabinet met in January, 1906.
And then he goes on further to say that all during 1906 and later he, as a member of

the cabinet, was not made acquainted with these conversations which had taken place with the French and Belgian officers. Further, he asked the question-When did the war come, and how did they bring us into it? Speaking with regard to the action of the ministers of the Crown, he says:
The answer to this question, in & single sentence, is that we were brought into the war because Mr. Asquith and Sir Edward Grey and their confidants, by steps some of which are known while others may be unknown, had placed us in such a position toward France, and therefore also toward Russia, that they found they could not refuse to take up arms on her behalf when it came to the issue, though till the end they denied it to parliament, and probably even to themselves.

Does the hon. gentleman suggest that England was in honour bound to go and support France when she went to war, and that Canada is not in honour bound to go and support England if she ||ot into difficulties.

I suggest that owing to this series of conversations and arrangements that took place between England and France prior to the last war, without there being any written treaties or conventions with the consent of parliament thereto, and without the knowledge of the whole cabinet, Britain found herself so involved that, without loss of honour, she could not stay out of the war. As I proceed further with my argument, my hon. friend will see that it is to avoid any such contingency arising in Canadian politics, that this resolution is being brought down this evening.

May I ask the hon. gentleman a question which is relevant to the present theme of his discussion? Was the government of Canada justified, in August, 1914, at the time Great Britain entered the war, in pledging Canada's active military support to Britain without securing the consent of the parliament of Canada?

I am under the impression that owing to some more of those conversations, for instance the interchange of officers between the British general staff and our exchange of officers, and also owing to a certain resolution passed unanimously in this House of Commons in 1909, we were practically pledged to go to war in case the British Empire was forced into war through aggression on the part of Germany. It is to prevent any such contingency in future without the know-_ ledge and full consent of parliament, that this resolution is being introduced.
Before closing that portion of my remarks relating to how Britain entered the war, let me read Lord Loreburn's appreciation of Sir

Edward Grey's speech on the 3rd August, 1914:
0 -
This remarkable speech began with an elaborate effort to prove that the House of Commons was perfectly free to determine either for peace or war. It ended with a passionate declaration that this country would be disgraced if we did not declare war, and the reasoning of the speech proved that Sir Edward Grey had committed himself irretrievably.
As I said before, this is a case where a great nation, the greatest nation on earth, a nation which has amongst its statesmen those who should be most familiar with everything that goes on in international politics, a nation the members of whose House of Commons probably study international politics more than those of any other similar bodies in the world, found that it had restrained its liberty of action in case of an aggressive war on the part of Germany to such an extent that it could not remain out of the war without, as I said before, besmirching the nation's honour. If such a thing can happen with regard to England, how much more so could it happen with regard to this country? Our leaders, much as I admire and respect them, will be, I think, the very first to admit that they have possibly not the training in diplomacy, nor in the knowledge of old-world events, which the members of the British cabinet and the members of the House of Commons of Britain, before 1914, possessed. As I said before, the general aim and object of this resolution is to prevent this country from being placed in a position similar to that which Great Britain was placed in before 1914. The resolution really only gives a more general application to, and elaborates an amendment moved by the right hon. the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) when he was leader of the Opposition, on April 27, 1921, on' the occasion of the departure of the present leader of the Opposition (Mr. Meighen) then Prime Minister for Great Britain to attend the Prime Ministers' conference. The original motion stated that it was advisable to take part in the Imperial Conference, and so forth; and the present Prime Minister moved:
That the House, while recognizing the propriety of Canada being represented at any Imperial conference or conference of the Prime Ministers of the Empire that may be called, desires to record its opinion that at the coming conference no step should be taken in any way involving any change in the relations of Canada to other parts of the Empire; and that, in view of the present financial position of Canada, no action should be taken implying any obligations on the part of Canada to undertake new expenditures for naval or .military purposes.
This amendment was defeated by some thirty votes. But may I say now to the right hon. the leader of the Opposition (Mr. Meighen) that, though he considered it his duty at the time to ask his supporters to vote down this amendment, he took to heart the injunctions which had been given him, and by his manly stand and his steadfast Cana-dianism was able to resist the blandishments of the Imperialists and prevent the renewal of the Japanese Treaty. The principles enunciated in that resolution remain, I think, the principles which guide the Liberal party in its foreign and imperial policy to-day. There can be no objection, then, on the part of the government to accepting the more general statement as outlined in the resolution which I have placed on the order paper. There will no doubt be other imperial conferences; there will be other discussions of the question of imperial defence; and our ministers, when discussions relating to these matters arise, might very well be pleased to be able to say to those who approach them that it is useless to converse, useless to negotiate, unnecessary to enter into undertakings because their hands are tied, they are bound by a resolution of the Canadian House of Commons not in any way to commit their country to any participation whatsoever without previously having consulted parliament. This, I submit, would be in the best interests of the ministers themselves; it would make the matter clear for everyone; and it would be following out the adage of which so much was said during the war,-open agreements, open covenants, openly arrived at. I can conceive of the case where it might be necessary for two nations which are combining against the aggression of a third party to keep secret the negotiations and even the result of their combination. It might be that this very combination might be sufficient to urge the third nation into making an attack before the plans of the other two parties were completed. But in this country we need no such precaution; we need have no enemies on this continent; and we have no right to make enemies for ourselves on any other continent. Any arrangements which the representatives of the people of Canada may arrive at should be arrived at in the broad light of day and be freely published, so that every citizen of the Dominion may know just to what he is obliged and under what circumstances he may act in such and such a matter. To sum up, I have tried-
Does the hon. gentleman think, in the event of enemy attacking Great Britain and being victorious, that Canada would be free from the penalties of the loser?

I am rather under the impression that we would. It has been said
Canada and War

quite freely that in any case in which Great Britain is at war, whether we want to go to war or not, we would be attacked. I think the hon. gentleman knows, and every hon. gentleman in this House ought to know, that it would not be to the advantage of any single nation on earth to make an enemy of Canada if Canada were not inclined to go into war. Almost any nation on earth would carefully refrain from attacking a country which could put 500,000 of the best fighting troops in the world in the field at practically a moment's notice.
Now, I have tried to show that at the present moment our slate is clean in so far as international or imperial obligations are concerned. I have tried to show also that there is a way of keeping that slate clean. The passing of a resolution such as this is one way that would keep us from undertaking any entangling al- liances or engagements. It remains only for me to close my observations by stating that my motives in bringing forward this resolution are not anti-British any more than they are anti-American. They are simply Canadian. I am Canadian, purely and simply, and I place the interests of this country before those of any other country no matter how closely we may be related thereto. A number of hon. gentlemen in this House may have arrived at the same conclusions as I have reached, but by following different paths. With these I have no quarrel, any more than I have any quarrel with those who think I am utterly and absolutely wrong. This is a matter of opinion. The question of our relations to the Empire is, I think, one of the greatest questions now before the people of Canada. It is certainly one question on which we can have a definite line of cleavage, at any rate. At the present time, for instance, with regard to the tariff, we have free traders and protectionists on this side of the House, and we have protectionists and so-called free traders on the other side. And we have private ownership and public ownership advocates sitting cheek by jowl on either side of the House. On almost every single question it is possible to cut clear across party lines. But on this question the time is fast approaching when every citizen of Canada will have to decide whether he is a Canadian first or a Britisher first. And when that question is placed before the people of Canada, without any extraneous circumstances to dim their vision or prejudice their judgment, then I think every member of this House will have to make his choice one way or the other. I think from what I have said to-night the House knows where my choice will lie. It will

be said perhaps that the views which I have expressed this evening are selfish and narrow. To their selfishness I plead guilty; I think we should be selfish with regard to our country. We should so take the interest of our country to heart that we have little time or occasion to be worried over the fortunes of any other country.
It will be said too, that my views are narrow. But how can views be narrow which take into consideration the problems of the miner from Nova Scotia, of the farmer from Alberta and of the fisherman from British Columbia? We have national problems great enough to exercise the minds of our ablest statesmen. We have class problems-the problem of the employer, the problem of the worker, the problem of the farmer, the problem of the manufacturer; we have the problems of race antagonism and religious prejudice; we have economic problems-our railways are on our hands and we have to seek some means of developing our national resources. When we have settled, if ever we do settle, these problems, it will be time enough for us to turn our attention to the woes of the Hindu, to the troubles of the Australian sheep-rancher,, to the hardships of the tax-burdened Lancashire miner, to the sorrows of the London coster. But until such time as we have either settled definitely or come to some conclusion regarding the settlement of these great national problems which cry aloud for solution, I say our people should devote their attention to their own national affairs, in an endeavour to make this country more prosperous and better to live in, and indeed a country better than any other in all the world.

On that score he certainly deserves the thanks of every patriotic person in this country.
Members sitting in this House and having a leaning towards militarism or imperialism can no more parade as drawing room generals, or seriously cast a shadow of doubt on the
